risk_of_bias.note: The figures on recovery without treatment are second-hand from a review that did not appraise its 27 studies, 71 of whose 124 estimates the reviewers calculated themselves (card sc_mellor_2019: narrative-review checklist, high); the meta-analysis reports no appraisal of its cohorts and pools follow-ups of 3 to 50 years with a lifetime survey estimate (card sc_fleury_2016: AMSTAR 2 critically low); the figures for drug dependence in the US surveys are a reviewer's own calculations from published prevalences and from curves and unpublished yearly figures the survey's authors supplied, without intervals, from single interviews that miss people in jails and prisons and people who had died (card sc_heyman_2013: narrative-review checklist, high); the Vietnam study rests on self-report, study-specific criteria, a window of about a year in its first report and a 95% figure without a denominator (card sc_robins_1975: JBI moderate), and its three-year and treatment figures come from the principal investigator's lecture, which gives no denominators or definitions and whose text and graphs disagree in places (card sc_robins_1993: narrative-review checklist, high); in the national survey of alcohol dependence, offset includes people with residual symptoms and 20% were not re-interviewed (card sc_verges_2012). A claim seen through reviews is downgraded for risk of bias (METHODS 6.3).

inconsistency.note: Estimates range from 2.7% to 98.3%, but the alcohol review shows that the range follows mostly from the denominator and the definitions, and every source finds remission common on its own terms; the four US surveys agree closely (76% to 83% under the same rule, 57% under a stricter one). Not downgraded, because the statement ties each figure to its definition and sample.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: each figure is given with its population (US adults in national surveys, 1980–2003; young US enlisted men in 1971–1974; US adults with alcohol dependence in 2001–2005; mostly treatment-recruited cohorts; mostly North American alcohol studies); the statement says that remission meant not meeting the criteria in the past year, not quitting, and was counted drug by drug in the analyses by drug, that heroin and other opioids are not among the drugs in those analyses, and that no source read counted recovery without treatment for drugs other than alcohol.

imprecision.note: Large samples behind the survey figures (no intervals printed); the Vietnam figures for dependence after return rest on small numbers (about 4 to 5 men dependent after return in the general sample) and approximate readings of a figure, stated as such.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for descriptive survey figures; the alcohol review included every numeric estimate it found, whatever its size.

rate.reasoning: Descriptive claim: starts low and is rated as a description of the samples. Down one for risk of bias, because the part of the question about recovery without treatment rests on second-hand, unappraised estimates (and on a meta-analysis of unappraised, mostly treatment-recruited cohorts), and the survey figures for drugs are a reviewer's recalculations: very low. A lenient reading would rate the Vietnam and national-survey figures alone (primary data from a near-complete random sample and weighted national surveys) as low for the narrower statement that many people no longer meet the criteria within one to three years; the rating is set by the weakest necessary link. Not upgraded (descriptive). Status replicated: the direction holds in independent samples (the Vietnam veterans; the US national surveys; the cohorts pooled by Fleury et al.), but the 2001–02 US survey (NESARC) appears in several places: Heyman's survey figure and his curves by drug, which come from the same remission analysis (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011, in Addiction) that Fleury et al. pooled as their lifetime estimate; Vergés et al.; Moss et al. (2010), a general-population sample from the same survey followed for three years, in Fleury et al.; and Dawson et al. in Mellor et al.; these are not counted as independent of each other, and the Vietnam cohort's 1975 report and 1993 lecture are one study. Not used: Heyman's comparison of treated and untreated Vietnam veterans, which joins figures for different groups and time spans; his conclusions that remission does not require treatment and that most people stop by about age 30, which go beyond what the surveys measured; the 95% remission rate as a figure (no stated denominator), Fleury et al.'s annual remission rates (inconsistent with its pooled proportions), its 14 years of use before remission (not derivable from its table) and its conservative-rate comparison by treatment at entry (not reproducible from its study values), and Mellor et al.'s medians as rates (card reporting issues). The comparison of cohorts by treatment at entry describes who entered each study, not who recovered without treatment, and the low share of people in treatment in the surveys describes current cases, not who recovered without it.
rate.population: US adults in four national surveys of psychiatric disorders (Epidemiologic Catchment Area 1980–84, nearly 20,000 people in five metropolitan areas, prisons included; National Comorbidity Survey 1990–92, about 8,100; its replication 2001–03, about 9,200; NESARC 2001–02, about 43,000), as recalculated in a review (Heyman, 2013); US Army enlisted men returning from Vietnam in September 1971, interviewed 8 to 12 months later (451 in a random general sample; 898 in both samples) (Robins et al., 1975) and about 3 years after return (Robins, 1993); US adults in a national household survey interviewed in 2001–2002 and 2004–2005 (34,653 re-interviewed; 1,172 of them with past-year alcohol dependence at the first interview, an editors' sum) (Vergés et al., 2012); 21 studies of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders published 2000–2015 (20 cohorts, 15 recruited through treatment, and one national survey's lifetime estimate) (Fleury et al., 2016); 27 studies of untreated remission from alcohol problems, 1976–2018, mostly North American (Mellor et al., 2019)
rate.exposure: Having had an alcohol or drug problem (DSM drug dependence as each survey diagnosed it, with abuse and dependence combined in the oldest survey; dependence on cocaine, cannabis, alcohol or cigarettes, drug by drug; narcotic dependence or addiction in Vietnam, self-reported or by the study's own criteria; DSM-IV alcohol dependence; substance use disorders as each cohort diagnosed them; alcohol problems as each study defined them), with or without treatment as each study defined it
rate.comparator: None (descriptive); the same people's earlier status; in the alcohol review, three different denominators (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, people already recovered)
rate.outcome: No longer meeting the criteria for the problem (remission) at a later interview or at the last follow-up, as each study defined it (not meeting dependence criteria in the past year, meaning two or fewer dependence symptoms, or no symptoms in the oldest survey; time from the start of dependence to remission, drug by drug; not dependent again within about a year, and not addicted again within 3 years, in the Vietnam veterans; not meeting full DSM-IV criteria in the year before an interview about three years later; at least six months without meeting criteria; abstinence or moderate drinking), and the share of it without treatment
rate.magnitude: Heyman (2013), share of lifetime drug dependence not current in the past year, from published lifetime and 12-month prevalences (no intervals): ECA 1980–84 57% (abuse and/or dependence; remission = no symptoms), NCS 1990–92 76%, NCS-R 2001–03 83%, NESARC 2001–02 81% (dependence; remission = two or fewer symptoms). NESARC curves from the onset of dependence, drug by drug: half remitted by about year 4 (cocaine), 6 (cannabis; year 7 on p. 48), 16 (alcohol) and about 30 (cigarettes); two-thirds by year 7 (cocaine), 27 (alcohol), 49 (cigarettes); at 10 years 79%, 69%, 40%, 20% and at 15 years 89%, 81%, 49%, 28% (cocaine, cannabis, alcohol, nicotine); dependent for at least 16 and 23 years 10% and 5% (cocaine), at least 23 and 36 years 10% and 5% (cannabis). Treatment: ECA at most 30% had mentioned drug use to a health specialist; NESARC no more than 16% of current cases in treatment. People in jails and prisons missed: remission about 80% falls to about 64% with a quarter more cases none of whom remitted (about 74% if half of them had stopped by about age 37). Robins (1993), men addicted in Vietnam: addicted again in the first year after return 5%, at any time in 3 years 12%; simple detoxification in service for a third; drug treatment after return entered by under 2% of men who used narcotics in Vietnam, 6% of men positive at departure and 14% of those positive at departure who kept using; two-thirds of treated men relapsed by the time of interview. Robins et al. (1975), general sample N=451, before / in / since Vietnam: narcotic use 11% / 43% / 10%; dependence self-reported 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%, by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%. Still dependent at departure (both samples pooled, no weighting stated, n=134): 50% used narcotics after return, 14% dependent again. A period of more-than-weekly narcotic use since return 3% vs under 0.5% before service. Men first dependent in Vietnam dependent again 8–10 months after return (Figure, approximate): about 2% (general sample, N=90) and about 7% (urine-positive sample, N=341). Stated remission rate 95% (no denominator). Vergés et al. (2012), NESARC 2001–2002 to 2004–2005: 422 of 1,172 with past-year alcohol dependence (36%) dependent again about three years later, about 64% (750) not (1,172 = 422 + 750, and both shares are editors' calculations, unweighted); weighted persistence 32.4% (ages 21–23) and 44.5% (43–52). Fleury et al. (2016), 21 studies (20 cohorts, follow-up 3–50 years, and one lifetime survey estimate entered as 95.7%): standard remission 54.4% (95% CI 42.1–66.2), studies 19.6–95.7%, I² 99.4%; conservative 35.0% (25.2–46.4), I² 99.5%; without the lifetime survey, standard about 50.1% (42.5–57.6; editors' recalculation from Fig. 4, matching the lowest printed leave-one-out value) and conservative 30.9% (26.1–36.1, printed); treatment at baseline 51.1% vs not 62.4% (standard rate, p 0.421; about 48–49% for the five cohorts without treatment at baseline other than the lifetime survey, editors' recalculation; the printed conservative-rate subgroups could not be rebuilt from Fig. 4); standard rate higher with longer follow-up (B 0.046 per year, p 0.004) and lower retention (p 0.016), neither for the conservative rate. Mellor et al. (2019), alcohol, 124 estimates (71 calculated by the reviewers): 2.7% to 98.3%; nine studies with all three methods: all people with a problem 2.7–63.6%, untreated people 6.5–77.9%, remitted people 4.3–94.2% (6.4% with Table 3's values) (unweighted medians 12.4, 38.9 and 43.9, not rates); 78% of remitted people untreated (two Canadian surveys; abstinence or moderate drinking; 56.0% and 65.7% with abstinence only); 12.4% vs 32.6% of untreated people remitted (abstinence vs abstinence or moderate drinking; NESARC); 78% vs 40% of people untreated for three years in remission (any vs moderate or severe disorder; Netherlands); 36.0% vs 14.0% (remission at both 1 and 3 years vs also at 16 years; the 14.0% a reviewers' calculation; a US cohort).
rate.short: Many do. In US surveys, about 8 in 10 people who had ever been dependent on a drug no longer counted as dependent in the past year. Treatment was uncommon.
rate.rate: Big US surveys and long studies agree that many people recover. But most figures come second-hand, through reviews. And for drugs other than alcohol, nobody here counted who recovered without treatment.

risk_of_bias.note: Published case reports select severe, unusual or analytically interesting cases (seizures in about 38% of them against 4% in the one poison-centre series); the NBOMe was found in the person's own samples in only 15 of the 29 published cases (editors' count) and other drugs were often present; the features are not defined and the pooled shares cannot all be reproduced from the review's case descriptions; the review is not systematic and does not appraise its sources (card sc_wood_2015: some concerns).

inconsistency.note: The published cases and the poison-centre series differ in how often seizures were recorded, a difference the statement gives and that selection explains; the reports agree on the kind of features.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: the case reports, the poison-centre series and the European reports were not read; everything is as described by one narrative review (METHODS §6.3).

imprecision.note: Counts of reports, not rates; the shares rest on 29 and 25 cases, which the statement gives.

publication_bias.note: The selection of published cases is counted under risk of bias and not twice.

rate.reasoning: Descriptive (what was reported, and in which kind of data): starts low as case reports and record series seen through a narrative review; downgraded one level for risk of bias (selected, partly unconfirmed cases, often with other drugs) and one for indirectness (second-hand), bounded at very low; never upgraded. Because every supporting anchor cites one narrative review, the claim stays a draft and its statement says that its figures are second-hand. Status single study: one review; the primary reports it gathers come from different teams but were not read here, so they are not counted as independent replications. The statement gives the review's printed shares, not the editors' recount, and says that they are approximate; it reports deaths with the drug found or reported, not deaths caused by it. Nothing here measures how often blotters sold as LSD hold an NBOMe, the risk of harm from a use, or harm compared with LSD.
rate.population: People with reported poisoning or death after NBOMe use, 2010–2014, as gathered in one narrative review: 29 published poisoning cases (several known only from conference abstracts), 25 cases reported to Texas poison centres in 2012–2013, 25 non-fatal cases reported to the EU Early Warning System, and 8 reported deaths (forensic reports, the EU Early Warning System and a news report); first detections of NBOMes in Europe, 2011–2013
rate.exposure: NBOMe drugs (mostly 25I-NBOMe; also 25B- and 25C-NBOMe), reported by the person or found by laboratory analysis of the person's samples or of the product, often with other drugs; the forms in which they were found or taken (blotters, powder, liquid, capsules), including blotters taken as LSD or 'acid'
rate.comparator: None: case reports and one poison-centre series with no comparison group; the review sets the published cases beside the poison-centre series; no comparison with LSD
rate.outcome: Clinical features, severe complications and deaths as reported, whether the drug was confirmed by laboratory analysis, and cases in which people believed they had taken LSD
rate.magnitude: Wood et al. (2015), second-hand: first detections in Europe 2011–2013, 8 of 10 on blotters (editors' count, Table 1). 29 published poisoning cases (25I 23, 25B 3, 25C 3): tachycardia 96.6%, hypertension 62.0%, agitation/aggression 48.2%, seizures 37.9%, hyperthermia 27.6%, acute kidney injury 5 patients (as printed; editors' count from the case descriptions: seizures 12 of 29, kidney injury 6); NBOMe found in the person's own samples in 15 of 29, product only 2, no linked analysis 12 (editors' count). Texas poison centres 2012–2013, 25 cases: tachycardia 52%, agitation/irritability 48%, hallucinations 32%, hypertension 32%, confusion 24%, mydriasis 20%, seizures 4% (1 of 25, editors' calculation) against 38% in published cases. Deaths: 8 reported with 25I-NBOMe (abstract: detected in all 8); laboratory detection in 5, none reported for 3. Global Drugs Survey 2013 (22,289; non-representative): ever used an NBOMe 2.6%, LSD 39.4%. No denominators of people who used NBOMes; no rates or intervals.
rate.short: Yes, sometimes. NBOMes are lab-made drugs, mostly sold on blotters. In case reports up to 2014, several people who got sick or died thought they'd taken LSD.
rate.rate: One review of case reports up to 2014. Case reports pick out people who got very sick, only about half had the drug found in their own samples, and nobody counted everyone who used NBOMes.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence checklist moderate (card sc_maust_2019): a national probability sample, one instrument across both years and design-based weights, with a private computer section for drug questions; but everything is self-report without checks, response rates are not given, and misuse is defined broadly, putting taking extra of one's own prescription, taking a relative's pill to sleep and taking one to get high in one category, which the statement says. Under-reporting and non-response would more likely lower the misuse figure than change the order of reasons or sources. Not downgraded.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: US adults living in households in 2015–2016, and benzodiazepines in general (three in four people who misused one had misused alprazolam), not Xanax alone and not other countries.

imprecision.note: 2,533 people reporting misuse and 86,186 respondents; intervals are narrow for the overall figures. The figures for ages 50 or older rest on 176 people and are given only as a comparison.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to an analysis of a national survey.

rate.reasoning: Descriptive (prevalence, and self-reported reasons and sources, in a national survey): starts low and is never upgraded; not downgraded (see the domain notes). The reasons are people's own answers to a list and are worded as such; their printed shares add to 103.6%, which the statement says, so they cannot be read as exactly one reason per person, but the order (relaxing, then sleep, then getting high) does not depend on the extra 3.6 points. The associations with other substances are cross-sectional and show nothing about cause. The authors' suggestion that some misuse reflects poor access to care is given as their untested suggestion. The abstract's advice to monitor patients also prescribed opioids or stimulants is left out, because the paper's own Table 2 does not support it (prescribed opioid use went with lower odds of misuse, prescribed stimulant use with no difference). Status single study: one analysis of one survey's first two years after its redesign.
rate.population: US civilian adults aged 18 or older living in households, National Survey on Drug Use and Health 2015 and 2016 (86,186 respondents; 10,290 reporting past-year benzodiazepine use; 2,533 reporting misuse, 2,357 of them aged 18 to 49 and 176 aged 50 or older); people in institutions and on active military duty not covered
rate.exposure: Self-reported past-year benzodiazepine use, only as prescribed or with misuse (any use other than as a doctor directed: without a prescription, or in greater amounts, more often or longer than prescribed), reported in the survey's tranquilizer and sedative sections
rate.comparator: None for the shares among people reporting misuse (descriptive); use only as prescribed, for the share of use that was misuse and for the factors that went with misuse; ages 18 to 49 against 50 or older
rate.outcome: Self-reported past-year use and misuse; among people reporting misuse, its type, main reason (from a list), source and the benzodiazepine misused; days of misuse in the past month; DSM-IV abuse and dependence
rate.magnitude: Maust et al. (2019), NSDUH 2015–2016, survey-weighted: past-year any use 12.6% (95% CI 12.2–12.9), 30.6 million adults a year (29.7–31.5 million); only as prescribed 10.4% (10.1–10.7), 25.3 million (24.5–26.1); misuse 2.2% (2.0–2.3), 5.3 million (5.0–5.6); misuse 17.2% of use. Misuse by age, all adults: 18–25 5.2% (4.8–5.6), 26–34 3.3%, 35–49 1.7%, 50–64 1.4%, 65 or older 0.6% (0.4–0.8); as a share of use 51.0%, 28.6%, 13.8%, 9.7% and 4.4%. Among 2,533 reporting misuse (Table 3): without a prescription 73.9%, in greater amounts 16.0%, more often 10.1%, longer 4.9%, other ways 18.7%. Main reason: relax or relieve tension 47.1%, help with sleep 26.6%, get high 11.6%, feelings or emotions 10.1%, experiment 6.0%, effects of another drug 1.6%, hooked 0.6% (sum 103.6%, editors' calculation); ages 18–49 against 50 or older: get high 13.9% against 3.0% (OR 0.19, p = .003; interval printed as .07 to 56), sleep 22.4% against 41.7% (OR 2.48, 1.83–3.35), relax 48.6% against 41.7% (OR 0.76, 0.53–1.08). Source: free from a friend or relative 53.2%, bought from one 12.3%, stolen from one 3.3% (68.8%, editors' sum), one clinician 19.5%, two or more clinicians 0.9%, bought from a dealer or stranger 7.7%, stolen from a health care setting 0.1% (97.0% in all, editors' sum). Medication misused: alprazolam 75.1%, diazepam 20.5%, clonazepam 20.0%, lorazepam 15.4%. DSM-IV past-year abuse 4.6% (3.7–5.6), dependence 6.8% (5.6–8.2); mean days of misuse in the past month 5.4 (SE 0.3). Misuse against use as prescribed, adjusted OR: 65 or older against 18–25 0.23 (0.15–0.34); women 0.74 (0.61–0.90); alcohol abuse or dependence 2.31 (1.73–3.09); marijuana abuse or dependence 2.39 (1.62–3.52); prescription opioid misuse 4.11 (3.26–5.18), abuse or dependence 4.81 (3.45–6.72), use as prescribed 0.69 (0.57–0.84); prescription stimulant misuse 2.46 (1.85–3.27), abuse or dependence 3.40 (1.72–6.70), use as prescribed 0.90 (0.74–1.09).
rate.short: Mostly to relax or sleep, they say. In a big US survey, 47 in 100 people who misused benzos named relaxing as the main reason, 27 sleep, and 12 getting high.
rate.rate: One big national survey of US adults, chosen to stand for the whole country. But it's people's own answers, nobody checked them, and people in institutions such as prisons, or in the military, weren't asked.

risk_of_bias.note: Network meta-analysis: only 23.5% (children and adolescents) and 27.5% (adults) of the trials were at overall low risk of bias, most unclear; analyses restricted to low-risk trials or by sponsorship could not be done; the article reports no result of its funnel plots (AMSTAR 2 low confidence on card sc_cortese_2018). The blood-pressure review is of high AMSTAR 2 confidence, but 87 of its 102 trials were industry funded and its risk of bias enters only its certainty ratings. The head-to-head trial is at some concerns (RoB 2: randomization and missing-data handling not described, blind not checked, parent ratings on a scale without norms). One level, not two: the trials were double-blind and the reviews used unpublished data.

inconsistency.note: No significant global inconsistency for the primary outcomes of the first review (common heterogeneity SD 0.188 and 0.178 for clinician ratings, 0.268 and 0.282 for leaving because of side effects). In the blood-pressure review heterogeneity was low or low to moderate in children and adolescents and moderate or moderate to high in adults, with local incoherence in 2 of 12 comparisons for each blood pressure and 4 of 10 for pulse in children and adolescents; the comparisons the statement uses were not significant either way.

indirectness.note: The comparison between the two medicines rests largely on indirect comparison through placebo, and in adults entirely so (no trial comparing them in either network); 'amphetamines' pools several products (lisdexamfetamine included in the first review), while the head-to-head trial tested dexamphetamine at one fixed dose of each drug in children for two weeks; trials were short (median 7 weeks; analyses at about 12 weeks) at licensed or guideline doses. The statement is worded for short-term prescribed use in people with ADHD.

imprecision.note: The symptom intervals exclude no difference (−0.44 to −0.05; −0.54 to −0.05), though they reach small values; the children's blood-pressure intervals are narrow (systolic −2.33 to 0.44 mm Hg). The intervals for leaving because of side effects are wide (0.94 to 2.73; 0.54 to 3.43), and the statement says a difference is neither shown nor ruled out rather than calling the two equal; that comparison alone would be rated down for imprecision.

publication_bias.note: The blood-pressure review's contour-enhanced funnel plots did not indicate small-study effects; the first review's funnel plots are only in its appendix (counted under risk of bias). Both reviews sought unpublished data from manufacturers and regulators (83% of trials in the first review).

rate.reasoning: Randomized trials start high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1, indirectness −1; inconsistency, imprecision and publication bias 0. Low for the statement as worded: in short trials of prescribed medicines in people with ADHD, amphetamines gave a slightly larger reduction in clinician-rated symptoms than methylphenidate (the review's own GRADE: low in both age groups), while stopping because of side effects and rises in blood pressure and pulse were not shown to differ. Taken alone, the adult comparisons and the comparison of stopping would be very low (indirect only, or imprecise; the review rates the adult comparison of stopping very low), and the head-to-head trial's severity finding, one trial at one fixed dose of each drug with parent ratings on a scale without norms, would be low. Relation 'is associated with': the trials were randomized, but the comparison between the two drugs is mostly indirect, which is not a randomized comparison. Status single study: each finding rests on one source (symptoms and stopping on one network meta-analysis; blood pressure and pulse on a second that reused its searches and shares three authors; side-effect severity on one trial), and the trial-by-trial results are in appendices that were not read, so the trials inside the networks are not counted as independent replications here. Not rated: long-term effects, numbers of people who stop, psychosis (a separate answer) and use without a prescription.
rate.population: Children and adolescents aged 5 to 17 and adults with a primary diagnosis of ADHD in double-blind randomized trials of at least 1 week (133 trials to April 2017: 14,346 children and adolescents and 10,296 adults; 102 trials to January 2024: 13,315 children and adolescents, mean age 11, and 9387 adults, mean age 35, mostly from high-income countries; the two sets of trials overlap); and 125 children aged 5 to 15 (114 boys) with DSM-IV ADHD referred to a hospital clinic in Melbourne, 1995–1996
rate.exposure: Amphetamine medicines taken by mouth as prescribed for ADHD, at licensed or guideline doses (study conditions): 'amphetamines' including lisdexamfetamine in Cortese et al. (2018); amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine as separate groups in Farhat et al. (2025); dexamphetamine twice a day for 2 weeks at one fixed weight-based dose (0.15 mg/kg per dose) in Efron et al. (1997)
rate.comparator: Methylphenidate (including dexmethylphenidate in Cortese et al.), compared within networks of trials that mostly link the two through placebo (in adults only through placebo); placebo; in Efron et al., methylphenidate twice a day for 2 weeks (0.3 mg/kg per dose) in the same children in random order, and each child's own ratings before treatment (no placebo)
rate.outcome: Clinician-rated change in core ADHD symptoms (standardized mean difference) and leaving a trial because of side effects (odds ratio) at the time closest to 12 weeks, with teacher ratings, global improvement, acceptability and weight; change in systolic and diastolic blood pressure (mm Hg) and pulse (beats per minute) at the time closest to 12 weeks (median trial length 7 weeks); in the head-to-head trial, parents' ratings of 17 listed complaints (number and severity) and stopping because of severe adverse effects
rate.magnitude: Cortese et al. (2018), network estimates at the time closest to 12 weeks (GRADE from Tables 1 and 2). Clinician-rated core symptoms, SMD against placebo: amphetamines −1.02 (−1.19 to −0.85) children and adolescents, −0.79 (−0.99 to −0.58) adults; methylphenidate −0.78 (−0.93 to −0.62) and −0.49 (−0.64 to −0.35); all moderate. Amphetamines against methylphenidate −0.24 (−0.44 to −0.05) and −0.29 (−0.54 to −0.05), both low. Teachers' ratings: methylphenidate −0.82 (−1.16 to −0.48, low); no data for amphetamines. CGI-I: amphetamines and methylphenidate not significantly different (no estimate printed). Leaving because of side effects, OR against placebo: amphetamines 2.30 (1.36–3.89) and 3.26 (1.54–6.92), moderate; methylphenidate 1.44 (0.90–2.31, low) and 2.39 (1.40–4.08, high); amphetamines against methylphenidate 1.60 (0.94–2.73, low) and 1.36 (0.54–3.43, very low), values above 1 meaning more leaving on amphetamines. Acceptability against placebo: methylphenidate in children and adolescents 0.69 (0.52–0.91); amphetamines in adults 0.68 (0.49–0.95). Weight, SMD against placebo: amphetamines −0.71 (−1.15 to −0.27) and −0.60 (−1.03 to −0.18); methylphenidate −0.77 (−1.09 to −0.45) and −0.74 (−1.20 to −0.28). Trials 133 (81, 51, 1 both); participants 14,346 and 10,296; symptom analysis 10,068 and 8131; stopping analysis 11,018 and 5362. Farhat et al. (2025), mean difference against placebo at the time closest to 12 weeks (median 7 weeks), CINeMA certainty: children and adolescents, methylphenidate systolic 1.81 mm Hg (1.05 to 2.57, moderate), diastolic 2.42 (1.69 to 3.15, low), pulse 3.88 beats a minute (2.87 to 4.89 in Figure 3; 4.8 in the text and Figure 5; moderate); amphetamines 0.87 (−0.3 to 2.03, high), 1.93 (0.74 to 3.11, high), 1.78 (−0.12 to 3.69, moderate); lisdexamfetamine 1.76 (0.68 to 2.83, moderate), 2.29 (1.25 to 3.34, low), 4.17 (2.74 to 5.61, very low). Adults (all very low): methylphenidate 1.66 (0.38 to 2.93), 1.6 (0.29 to 2.91), 4.37 (3.16 to 5.59); amphetamines 2.3 (0.66 to 3.94), 1.91 (0.17 to 3.65), 5.18 (3.47 to 6.89); lisdexamfetamine 1.62 (−0.81 to 4.06), 3.07 (0.69 to 5.45), 5.07 (2.76 to 7.37). Amphetamines minus methylphenidate: systolic −0.94 (−2.33 to 0.44, high) and 0.64 (−1.44 to 2.72); diastolic as printed (methylphenidate minus amphetamines) 0.49 (−0.88 to 1.87, high) and −0.31 (−2.49 to 1.87); pulse −2.1 (−4.25 to 0.06) and 0.81 (−1.29 to 2.90). Lisdexamfetamine minus methylphenidate: systolic −0.06 (−1.17 to 1.06, moderate) and −0.04 (−2.79 to 2.71); diastolic as printed (methylphenidate minus lisdexamfetamine) 0.13 (−0.98 to 1.24, moderate) and −1.47 (−4.19 to 1.25); pulse 0.29 (−1.24 to 1.83, low) and 0.69 (−1.92 to 3.3). Figure 5 also marks amphetamines minus lisdexamfetamine pulse in children and adolescents as −2.39 (−4.78 to −0.01, low), which the text leaves out. Trials 102 (61 children and adolescents, 13,315 people; 41 adults, 9387); 87 industry funded; four with 24-week data, none longer. Efron et al. (1997), 125 children, parent ratings on 17 items (0 to 9): number of complaints, mean (SD), before 8.19 (3.97), dexamphetamine 7.64 (3.83), methylphenidate 7.19 (3.82), F(2,122) = 3.72, p = .03 (only before against methylphenidate significant at p < .01); mean severity 4.08 (1.56), 3.73 (1.68), 3.24 (1.46), F = 15.98, p < .01 (before against methylphenidate and dexamphetamine against methylphenidate significant). Item severity, before, dexamphetamine, methylphenidate: trouble sleeping 2.21, 3.61, 2.69; poor appetite 1.22, 2.74, 2.12; irritability 4.57, 3.65, 2.94; proneness to crying 3.35, 3.4, 2.7; anxiousness 3.94, 2.71, 2.07; sadness or unhappiness 2.86, 2.43, 1.69; nightmares 1.09, 0.79, 0.48. Counts of 125 before, on dexamphetamine and on methylphenidate: poor appetite 43, 74, 69; trouble sleeping 67, 88, 79; irritability 102, 102, 100; anxiousness 96, 85, 76. rate.short: Both work. In a review of 133 short trials, amphetamine (as in Adderall) eased symptoms a bit more than methylphenidate (Ritalin). Neither clearly made more people quit over side effects.
rate.rate: Two big reviews of trials, but few trials tested the two drugs against each other, and none in adults. Trials lasted weeks, and most were paid for by drug makers.

risk_of_bias.note: Registered, randomized, counterbalanced, double-dummy crossover with complete data for all 28 (N = 28 and F(4,108) in every supplementary table; card sc_holze_2022: RoB 2 some concerns). People named the right drug after 71 to 86 in 100 sessions and the dummy after every session (editors' calculation from Supplementary Table S8), so every subjective outcome, including the duration, which is modelled from self-ratings, was rated by people who often knew which drug they had; sequence generation and concealment are not described; the results text contradicts Supplementary Table S5 on heart rate after LSD 100 µg, two printed means lie outside their ranges, and 99 outcomes were each tested pairwise without correction across outcomes (editors' count of Table 1 and Supplementary Tables S1–S5). Blood pressure, heart rate and temperature are objective.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: pure psilocybin in capsules and LSD in solution, single study doses, healthy screened volunteers with little drug experience in a hospital room, which the statement says. It claims nothing about mushrooms, other doses or settings, and gives no matching amounts.

imprecision.note: 28 people. The duration difference is large and its test decisive, but 'no difference in kind' rests on non-significant post hoc tests without equivalence margins (Supplementary Tables S1–S4), and the differences in blood pressure, heart rate and temperature between the drugs are a few mmHg, a few beats a minute or a few tenths of a degree (Supplementary Table S5).

rate.reasoning: Randomized, counterbalanced within-person comparison: starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias −1 (self-ratings under weak blinding between the two drugs, a results text that contradicts its own supplementary table, misprinted values) and imprecision −1 (28 people; sameness in kind cannot be shown without equivalence testing) give low. The duration difference on its own (about 9 to 11 hours against 6 to 7, in the same people, with a decisive test and a plausible link to the half-lives) would be rated moderate, held down only by the self-rated outcome; the statement that the experiences were alike in kind would be rated low or lower, and is worded as not shown either way. Status single study: the first within-person comparison, from one laboratory. The authors' dose-equivalence figures rest on doses not given in this study and are not used; no comparison of strength is made. The online supplement, read in round pdf-2026-11-26, gives the peak values, the guesses and the complaint counts; it does not change the rating.
rate.population: 28 healthy, screened adults (14 women, 14 men; mean age 35, range 25 to 52), recruited by word of mouth or from a pool of people interested in psychedelic trials, and paid; 14 had used a psychedelic before and 10 had never used an illicit drug other than cannabis; excluded were a personal or first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder, interfering medicines and more than 10 lifetime uses of illicit drugs (cannabis excepted); Basel
rate.exposure: Single oral doses of LSD base as a solution, labelled 100 and 200 µg (analysed content 84.5 µg per 100 µg unit), given double-blind and double-dummy in a calm hospital room with one investigator, in random, counterbalanced order with at least 10 days between sessions (study conditions)
rate.comparator: Psilocybin 15 and 30 mg in capsules (analysed 4.61 mg per 5 mg capsule) and placebo, in the same people on other days
rate.outcome: Duration and onset of self-rated effects (modelled from 'any drug effect' ratings); peak self-ratings on visual analogue scales, the 5D-ASC (primary outcome, rated at 24 hours), mystical-experience and mood scales; blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and pupil size; complaint scores for 0 to 12 and 12 to 24 hours and adverse events within 48 to 72 hours; guesses of which drug was given
rate.magnitude: Holze et al. (2022), 28 people. rate.short: Mostly how long it lasts: about 9 to 11 hours for LSD, 6 to 7 for psilocybin, the drug in mushrooms. Otherwise 28 lab volunteers rated the trips alike on most measures.
rate.rate: One careful lab study of 28 people, who took both drugs in random order. But most could tell which drug they had, and 'alike' only means no clear difference was found.

risk_of_bias.note: Seen only through a narrative review by the authors of the studies (card sc_greenwald_2014: narrative-review checklist high; no search, the authors' own studies re-analysed by them). The primary studies cannot be appraised from the review; as it describes them, doses were given in a fixed order (2, 16, then 0 mg; 32, 16, 2, 0 mg), the time course after stopping is referenced to other people's placebo scans, the Comer estimates come from a model fitted to behaviour against a separate placebo group, and values between scans are curve fits.

inconsistency.note: The studies point the same way (availability falling with dose and rising after stopping; blockade incomplete at every dose studied); imaging and modelling give different figures, which the authors say should not be compared.

indirectness.note: Second-hand; volunteers dependent on heroin, not in treatment, mostly men, relatively healthy; fentanyl was not studied; receptor availability and laboratory self-administration stand in for what people ask (whether other opioids work, and the risk of using them), and no breathing or overdose outcome is reported.

imprecision.note: 3, 5 and 10 people in the scan studies and 7 against 8 in the modelling study; no intervals or tests are printed for any availability figure.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the review selected the authors' own studies.

rate.reasoning: As the review describes them, the primary studies are within-person comparisons with placebo given in a fixed order, a time course without a concurrent control and a comparison with a separate group, so the evidence starts low (METHODS 6.3: within-person laboratory studies start high only when the order was randomized or counterbalanced, and a claim seen only through reviews starts from the design of the primary studies). Down one level each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision: very low (the floor is reached at the first downgrade; the others are recorded for their reasons). The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft and its statement says the figures are second-hand (METHODS 6.3). Status replicated by the same team: the fall in availability with dose was seen in two scan studies (3 and 5 people) and incomplete blockade in several studies, all by overlapping authors; the time course after stopping rests on one study of 10 people. The abstract's thresholds are reported as the authors' inferences, not as findings. The doses are the studies' conditions; the claim gives no dosing advice and no timing for using other opioids.
rate.population: People dependent on heroin who were not seeking treatment, studied as inpatients in laboratory studies by the review's authors, as described in one narrative review: 3 men (Zubieta et al., 2000), 5 volunteers (Greenwald et al., 2003), 10 volunteers (Greenwald et al., 2007; 5 heavier and 5 lighter smokers) and 7 volunteers on buprenorphine with naloxone against a separate group of 8 on placebo (Comer et al., 2005); in the scan studies aged 18 to 50, many fewer women than men, relatively healthy, without depressive, psychotic or anxiety disorders or substance use disorders other than nicotine
rate.exposure: Daily sublingual buprenorphine given by the investigators (study conditions: a liquid at 2 and 16 mg a day in Zubieta et al., 2000; buprenorphine-only tablets at 32, 16 and 2 mg a day, 12 days each, in Greenwald et al., 2003; 16 mg a day for at least 14 days, then placebo, in Greenwald et al., 2007; buprenorphine with naloxone at 2/0.5, 8/2 and 32/8 mg a day, 14 days each, in Comer et al., 2005), with test doses of intranasal heroin or injected hydromorphone given by the investigators; and time since the last dose after stopping 16 mg a day
rate.comparator: Placebo in the same people (Zubieta et al., 2000; Greenwald et al., 2003; doses given in a fixed order); the placebo condition of the 2003 study, in other people (Greenwald et al., 2007); a separate group of 8 heroin-detoxified volunteers on placebo (Comer et al., 2005); earlier against later times after the last dose
rate.outcome: Brain µ-opioid receptor availability (the share free to bind the PET tracer [11C]-carfentanil, as a percentage of placebo) 4 hours after the daily dose or 4 to 76 hours after the last dose; receptor availability estimated by a model from heroin self-administration and ratings (Comer et al., 2005); self-administration and subjective effects of heroin or hydromorphone; the availability thresholds for suppressing withdrawal and for blocking other opioids that the authors infer
rate.magnitude: Greenwald et al. (2014), the authors' summaries and re-analyses of their own studies; no intervals or test statistics printed. Availability, % of placebo, 4 hours after the daily dose: Zubieta et al. (2000; n = 3; liquid) 50–64% at 2 mg/day and 5–21% at 16 mg/day across regions; Greenwald et al. (2003; n = 5; tablets; range of means across seven regions) 53–72% at 2 mg, 9–20% at 16 mg, 2–12% at 32 mg; curve-fit estimates for doses not studied 71–85% (1 mg), 36–55% (4 mg), 20–35% (8 mg; 12–33% in the Fig. 1 legend), 13–24% (12 mg), 4–15% (24 mg). Heavier smokers (20 or more cigarettes a day, n = 5) had significantly lower availability than lighter smokers (15 or fewer, n = 5) in the 2007 study. rate.short: Only partly. In small lab studies, even high doses didn't fully block heroin or another opioid. After the last dose, scans over the next 3 days showed more opioid receptors free each day.
rate.rate: One review by the researchers who ran the studies, each with 3 to 10 volunteers, mostly men, all dependent on heroin. Receptor scans don't measure overdose risk, and fentanyl wasn't studied.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_senay_2003 (JBI, high): reports someone chose to make, to the manufacturer, the FDA or an informant network paid per questionnaire (average response 48.7%), of unknown completeness; much information missing (age known for 139 of 455, dose for 63 to 78 in 100, exposure for about half); the 'atypical' category created during the study and every case rescored without a check of agreement between raters; reports with drug-seeking moved to 'abuse'; no statistical analysis; funded by the manufacturer. inconsistency.note: One series; the Iranian case report titled as psychosis after stopping tramadol does not conflict with it.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the claim describes what reports contained and says that neither a frequency nor a comparison with other opioids was measured. A claim that tramadol withdrawal differs from that of other opioids would be rated lower.

imprecision.note: 422 rated reports (55 atypical) are enough to describe the reported pattern; the claim gives no frequency to be precise about.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; one surveillance programme reporting every case it classified.

rate.reasoning: Descriptive (what reported cases contained): starts low; down two levels for risk of bias; very low. Status single study: one surveillance series; the Iranian review adds two case reports and no study of how often withdrawal follows stopping. The rates per 100,000 are reported cases over estimated prescriptions, with a capture the authors themselves put at about 10 in 100 or less, so they are given only as minimums. Whether the 'atypical' symptoms are particular to tramadol was not tested: no group stopping another opioid was studied; and the abstract's nearly 40% is 33 in 100 by Table 3. rate.population: People in the USA prescribed tramadol (Ultram) in its first five years on the market (April 1995 to March 2000) whose withdrawal after stopping or reducing it was reported to the manufacturer, the FDA (MedWatch) or a paid network of 255 drug researchers, clinicians and counsellors; in Iran, two case reports (an adult and a newborn)

rate.comparator: None: no people who stopped tramadol without withdrawal and no people stopping another opioid; 'typical' and 'atypical' reports compared descriptively, 'atypical' defined against the DSM-IV list of opioid withdrawal symptoms
rate.outcome: Withdrawal as classified by the committee from reports: 'typical' opioid withdrawal (at least three DSM-IV opioid withdrawal symptoms, no drug-seeking) and 'atypical' withdrawal (opioid-type withdrawal with other nervous-system symptoms); the share of each symptom group among atypical cases; reported cases per 100,000 people estimated to be prescribed
rate.magnitude: Senay et al. (2003), adverse-event reports from April 1995 to March 2000: 1,248 classified; 422 rated withdrawal without drug-seeking (Table 3: 33%; editors' calculation 33.8%; abstract and Discussion: nearly 40%): typical 367 (86.97%), atypical 55 (13.03%; about 1 in 8; typical to atypical about 7 to 1); of 644 reports rated as 'abuse', 124 also had withdrawal symptoms (121 typical, 3 atypical), at least 546 in all (43.8% of 1,248, editors' calculation). Among the 55 atypical: severe anxiety and panic 32.8%, unusual CNS symptoms 27.2%, unusual sensory phenomena 25.4%, hallucinations 20.0% (as printed; the nearest counts of 55 give 32.7%, 27.3%, 25.5% and 20.0%, editors' calculation; the total exceeds 100%). rate.short: Sometimes, going by reports. In US reports from 1995 to 2000, most looked like usual opioid withdrawal. But about 1 in 8 also had panic, confusion, numbness or hallucinations.
rate.rate: One set of US side-effect reports, which catch only some cases, sorted by a committee the drug's maker paid for. Nobody compared people stopping tramadol with people stopping other opioids.

item.statement: Most people who were ever dependent on cocaine were still dependent decades later.
item.why: In a US survey, half had recovered within about 4 years, though some stayed dependent for decades. Recovery here means not counting as dependent for a year, not quitting.

lines.short: Many do. In US surveys, about 8 in 10 people who had ever been dependent on a drug no longer counted as dependent in the past year. Treatment was uncommon.
lines.but: That's not the same as quitting. And only alcohol studies counted who got better without treatment.
how: In three US surveys from 1990 to 2003, 76 to 83 in 100 people who had ever been dependent on a drug no longer counted as dependent in the past year. They could still use drugs, or relapse later.

Counted one drug at a time, half of people dependent on cocaine had recovered within about 4 years of becoming dependent, cannabis 6, alcohol 16 and cigarettes 30. Some stayed dependent for decades. Heroin wasn't in these figures.
Of US soldiers addicted to narcotics in Vietnam, 5 in 100 were addicted again in their first year home and 12 in 100 within 3 years. Few entered drug treatment back home.

In 21 long studies, mostly of people found through treatment, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen. For alcohol, counts of recovery without treatment run from about 3 to 98 in 100. That's mostly because studies count different groups.

item.statement: Blotters taken as LSD always hold LSD.
item.why: In some reported cases, blotters taken as 'acid' held an NBOMe instead. Nobody has counted how often this happens.

lines.short: Yes, sometimes. NBOMes are lab-made drugs, mostly sold on blotters. In case reports up to 2014, several people who got sick or died thought they'd taken LSD.
lines.but: Nobody has counted how often 'LSD' blotters hold NBOMes. And these are reports of people who got sick, so they can't say how risky one use is.
how: NBOMes are lab-made relatives of the 2C drugs. Of the first 10 found in Europe, from 2011 to 2013, 8 were on blotters. In some cases, blotters taken as 'acid' turned out to hold an NBOMe.
In 29 published cases of poisoning, nearly all had a racing heart and about 4 in 10 had seizures. Some needed intensive care, a breathing machine or dialysis.
Published cases are often the worst ones. Of 25 cases reported to Texas poison centres, 4 in 100 had seizures, against about 38 in 100 published cases.
By 2014, eight deaths had been reported with 25I-NBOMe, and a lab found it in five. Some had taken other drugs too. The review says its role in the deaths was often unclear.

item.statement: Most people who misuse benzos say they do it to get high.
item.why: In a big US survey, 12 in 100 named getting high as their main reason. Relaxing (47 in 100) and sleep (27) came first, by people's own account.

lines.short: Mostly to relax or sleep, they say. In a big US survey, 47 in 100 people who misused benzos named relaxing as the main reason, 27 sleep, and 12 getting high.
lines.but: It's what people told a survey. And 'misuse' here also counts taking more of your own pills than your doctor said.
how: In a US survey in 2015 and 2016, about 13 in 100 adults had used a benzo in the past year. About 2 in 100 had misused one. At ages 18 to 25, about half of all benzo use was misuse.
Misuse meant any use a doctor didn't direct. Most often (74 in 100) it was pills without a prescription. Three in four had misused alprazolam (Xanax).
Main reasons: relaxing 47 in 100, sleep 27, getting high 12, coping with feelings 10. These add up to a bit over 100, and the paper doesn't say why.
About 69 in 100 got the pills from a friend or relative, mostly for free, and 20 in 100 from one doctor. About 7 in 100 met the criteria for dependence.

item.statement: Scientists know just how much Suboxone it takes to block other opioids.
item.why: The researchers behind the brain scans say nobody knows. The levels in their summary came from early modelling of a few volunteers.

lines.short: Only partly. In small lab studies, even high doses didn't fully block heroin or another opioid. After the last dose, scans over the next 3 days showed more opioid receptors free each day.
lines.but: Each study had 3 to 10 volunteers on heroin, not in treatment. Fentanyl and overdose weren't studied.
how: In brain scans of people dependent on heroin, buprenorphine (Suboxone's main drug) took up more opioid receptors as the daily dose went up. At 16 mg a day, 9 to 20 in 100 were still free 4 hours after a dose.
Even at the highest doses tested, heroin and another opioid still had some effect. The review mentions people who take more of them to get past the block, but has no data on what happens then.
After 10 volunteers stopped 16 mg a day, free receptors rose from about 13 to 25 in 100 at 4 hours to about 75 to 90 in 100 at 3 days. These figures come from curves drawn between 4 scans.
The review's summary gives receptor levels needed to block other opioids. But its own authors say nobody knows them. A full block was never reliably seen.

item.statement: When people stop tramadol, it always feels like the usual opioid withdrawal.
item.why: In US reports from 1995 to 2000, about 1 in 8 cases also had panic, confusion, numbness or hallucinations. These were reported cases only, so how often it happens is unknown.

lines.short: Sometimes, going by reports. In US reports from 1995 to 2000, most looked like usual opioid withdrawal. But about 1 in 8 also had panic, confusion, numbness or hallucinations.
lines.but: It's only cases people chose to report. And no one compared it with stopping other opioids.
how: Of 1,248 side-effect reports in tramadol's first five years in the US, 422 were withdrawal after stopping. Most were the usual kind: cramps, diarrhoea, goose bumps, a runny nose, sweating, poor sleep.

55 (about 1 in 8) had more: bad anxiety or panic (1 in 3 of them), confusion or feeling unreal (1 in 4), numbness or tingling (1 in 4), or hallucinations (1 in 5). The researchers say this could be mistaken for psychosis.
Most people whose dose was known had taken no more than the recommended daily maximum, and many had used tramadol only a few days. Doctors called most cases mild, usually over in 2 or 3 days.

How often withdrawal happens is unknown: the researchers cite an estimate that only about 1 in 10 side effects get reported. The drug's maker paid for the study. A review of Iranian studies found just two case reports of it.

item.statement: Studies show people quit Adderall over side effects far more often than Ritalin.
item.why: Across short trials, quitting over side effects wasn't clearly different between amphetamine and methylphenidate, though a gap wasn't ruled out.

lines.short: Both work. In a review of 133 short trials, amphetamine (as in Adderall) eased symptoms a bit more than methylphenidate (Ritalin). Neither clearly made more people quit over side effects.
lines.but: Few trials tested the two head to head, and none in adults. Most compared one drug with a dummy pill, for a few weeks.
how: A review pooled 133 trials in about 14,300 children and teens and 10,300 adults. On doctors' ratings after about 12 weeks, amphetamine eased symptoms a little more than methylphenidate. The review rated this low certainty.

Quitting because of side effects wasn't clearly different between the two, but a gap wasn't ruled out. Against a dummy pill, more quit on amphetamine at every age, and on methylphenidate in adults. Both lowered weight.

Over about 7 weeks, blood pressure rose by about 1 to 3 points and heart rate by about 2 to 5 beats a minute on average, compared with a dummy pill. The two drugs didn't clearly differ, in 102 trials.

One blinded trial gave 125 children both, two weeks each, with no dummy pill. Parents counted as many complaints on each, but rated sleep and mood ones a bit worse on dexamphetamine, a kind of amphetamine. Many, like irritability (82 in 100), were there before any medicine.

item.statement: Given LSD or the drug in magic mushrooms without being told which, most people can't tell which one it was.
item.why: In a 28-person lab study, people named the right drug after 71 to 86 in 100 sessions, though they rated the trips alike on most measures.

lines.short: Mostly how long it lasts: about 9 to 11 hours for LSD, 6 to 7 for psilocybin, the drug in mushrooms. Otherwise 28 lab volunteers rated the trips alike on most measures.
lines.but: Finding no difference in 28 people doesn't prove there is none. And most could tell which drug they'd had.
how: 28 healthy adults each had five hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got a dummy, two amounts of LSD and two of psilocybin, in random order, not told which.
LSD lasted longer at both amounts. It also began a bit sooner, which the authors put down to it being a liquid, not a capsule.

The higher psilocybin amount raised blood pressure and body temperature a little more; the higher LSD amount raised heart rate more. On a checklist, 13 to 18 of the 28 had a headache in the first 12 hours after the drugs, against 8 on the dummy. Nobody had a serious problem.
People named the right drug after 71 to 86 in 100 sessions, and the dummy after every session, which may have shaped their ratings. It used pure psilocybin in capsules, not mushrooms.
