lines.statement: In people with alcohol or drug problems followed for between about a year and several decades, a large share no longer met the criteria for the problem at a later interview, but how many depends on who was counted (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, or people who had already recovered), on how a problem, recovery ('remission') and treatment were defined, and on the length of the time window; how many recovered without treatment was counted directly only in studies of alcohol problems, and for other drugs the sources read show only that treatment was uncommon. In four US national surveys of psychiatric disorders, most people who had ever met the criteria for drug dependence had not met them in the past year: 76% in the National Comorbidity Survey (1990–92), 83% in its replication (2001–03) and 81% in the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (2001–02), against 57% in the Epidemiologic Catchment Area survey (1980–84), which combined abuse with dependence and counted remission only when no symptoms remained, where the later surveys accepted two or fewer dependence symptoms (Heyman, 2013, the reviewer's own calculation from the surveys' published lifetime and past-year figures, without intervals). Remission meant not meeting the criteria in the past year, not quitting: a person counted as remitted could relapse the next year, and in the 2001–02 survey's analyses by drug it was counted one drug at a time, so a person in remission from cocaine dependence could be dependent on another drug (people who had remitted but met the criteria again at the interview were not counted as remitted). In those analyses, counted from the recalled start of dependence, half of the people ever dependent on cocaine had remitted by about year 4, on cannabis by about year 6 (year 7 elsewhere in the same review), on alcohol by year 16 and on cigarettes by about year 30; ten years after the start of dependence 79%, 69%, 40% and 20% had remitted, while 5% of people dependent on cocaine remained dependent for at least 23 years and 5% of those dependent on cannabis for at least 36; heroin and other opioids are not among the drugs analysed (Heyman, 2013, from the survey's published curves and yearly figures its authors supplied). Treatment was uncommon: in the 1980–84 survey at most 30% of people who had met the criteria said they had mentioned their drug use to a health specialist, and in the 2001–02 survey, with treatment defined broadly (from 12-step groups to methadone and religious counselling), no more than 16% of people who currently met the criteria were in treatment; by the reviewer's account, no analysis relating treatment to remission in such a population sample had been published by 2013. The surveys after 1984 did not sample people in jails and prisons; if there had been a quarter more people with drug dependence than the surveys counted (a published estimate the reviewer cites) and none of them had remitted, the remitted share would fall from about 80% to about 64% (the reviewer's calculation). Of 451 men interviewed from a random sample of 470 US Army enlisted men who returned from Vietnam in September 1971 (interviews 8 to 12 months after return), 43% had used narcotics there (about a third of the men had tried heroin) and 20% reported having been dependent on narcotics there (21% by the study's own criteria for dependence), against 10% who had used narcotics and 0.7% who reported dependence (1% by the criteria) since their return; of 134 men from the study's two samples who were still dependent when they left Vietnam, 50% used narcotics again after return and 14% were dependent again (the table's numbers add up to both samples together, with no weighting stated). The authors give a remission rate of 95% without saying which sample it describes; their figure, read approximately, shows that of the men first dependent in Vietnam, about 2% of 90 in the general sample and about 7% of 341 in a second sample (selected on a urine test at departure positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates) were dependent again. Remission there meant not being dependent again within about a year; many of the men counted as remitted still used narcotics, and a period of more-than-weekly narcotic use was more common after return than before Vietnam (3% against under 0.5%); men whose urine was positive at departure were to be held for detoxification and treatment, but the first report does not say how many men received drug treatment, before or after return; and the authors leave open whether the men's backgrounds or the change from Vietnam to home explains the remission (Robins et al., 1975). The principal investigator's later account of the same men gives 5% of those addicted in Vietnam as addicted in the first year after return and 12% at any time in the 3 years after return, and reports little treatment: only a third of the men addicted in Vietnam received even simple detoxification in service, and after return fewer than 2% of the men who had used narcotics in Vietnam entered drug treatment; she also writes that the conditions in Vietnam were unprecedented and that few of the men would have become addicted had they stayed in the US (Robins, 1993; see the answer on the Vietnam veterans). In a US national survey of adults interviewed in 2001–2002 and again about three years later (34,653 re-interviewed), 422 of the 1,172 people who had met the criteria for alcohol dependence in the year before the first interview met them again in the year before the second (36%), so about 64% did not (1,172 = 422 + 750, an editors' sum; both shares are editors' calculations from unweighted counts in a survey that over-sampled young adults and Black and Hispanic people, so they are not national estimates); in the paper's own weighted analysis, persistence was 32.4% at ages 21–23 and 44.5% at ages 43–52. Not meeting the full criteria can include people with one or two symptoms left, and treatment between the interviews is not reported (Vergés et al., 2012). A meta-analysis of 21 studies of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders, published 2000–2015 and mostly from the US (20 cohorts followed for 3 to 50 years, mean 17, 15 of them recruited through treatment, and one national survey that estimated remission over a lifetime), found 54% (95% CI 42% to 66%) of the people followed to the end in remission at the last follow-up, and 35% (25% to 46%) of everyone enrolled when deaths and people lost to follow-up were counted as not remitted; without the lifetime survey, about 50% (editors' recalculation) and 31%. Among the people followed to the end, single studies ranged from about 20% to 96%, the top value being the lifetime survey, and this rate, unlike the rate among everyone enrolled, was higher in cohorts followed longer and in cohorts that kept fewer of their participants. For treatment, the review compared cohorts only by whether people were in treatment when they entered, which cannot show who recovered without treatment: 51% with treatment at entry against 62% without (p 0.42), the six without including the lifetime survey (about 49% without it, editors' recalculation). Treatment during follow-up was not analysed, the pooled figures mix very different follow-up times and so describe no particular time point, the review reports no appraisal of its cohorts, and its authors read the results as showing that for many people these disorders are long-lasting (Fleury et al., 2016). For alcohol problems, a review of 124 estimates of recovery without treatment from 27 published studies (1976–2018, 24 of them North American; 71 of the estimates, the lowest among them, calculated by the reviewers from the studies' data) found figures from 2.7% to 98.3%, largely because the studies counted different things: among people already recovered, the share never treated (78% in two Canadian population surveys when recovery included moderate drinking, 56% and 66% when it meant not drinking); among people with an alcohol problem who stayed untreated, the share who recovered (in the US national survey of 2001–2002, 12.4% when recovery meant not drinking and 32.6% when moderate drinking also counted; in a Dutch survey, 78% of people with an alcohol use disorder who stayed untreated for three years were in remission at follow-up, against 40% of those whose disorder was moderate or severe; in one US cohort of people who had had no treatment beyond a single detoxification or a visit to an information and referral centre, 36.0% were in remission at both the 1- and 3-year follow-ups, and 14.0% when it also had to hold 16 years later); and among everyone with an alcohol problem, the share who recovered without treatment, which gave the lowest figures (2.7% to 63.6% in the nine studies that allowed all three counts). Most studies used a window of about one year, the review did not appraise the studies, and these figures are second-hand (Mellor et al., 2019). So a high share of never-treated people among those who recovered and a much lower share of everyone with a problem recovering without treatment in a year can both be right. For drugs other than alcohol, no source read here counted how many people recovered without treatment: the national surveys show that few people with current dependence were in treatment, and among the Vietnam veterans few men were treated and the principal investigator concludes that treatment did not explain the recovery. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: US adults in four national surveys of psychiatric disorders (Epidemiologic Catchment Area 1980–84, nearly 20,000 people in five metropolitan areas, prisons included; National Comorbidity Survey 1990–92, about 8,100; its replication 2001–03, about 9,200; NESARC 2001–02, about 43,000), as recalculated in a review (Heyman, 2013); US Army enlisted men returning from Vietnam in September 1971, interviewed 8 to 12 months later (451 in a random general sample; 898 in both samples) (Robins et al., 1975) and about 3 years after return (Robins, 1993); US adults in a national household survey interviewed in 2001–2002 and 2004–2005 (34,653 re-interviewed; 1,172 of them with past-year alcohol dependence at the first interview, an editors' sum) (Vergés et al., 2012); 21 studies of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders published 2000–2015 (20 cohorts, 15 recruited through treatment, and one national survey's lifetime estimate) (Fleury et al., 2016); 27 studies of untreated remission from alcohol problems, 1976–2018, mostly North American (Mellor et al., 2019)
lines.exposure: Having had an alcohol or drug problem (DSM drug dependence as each survey diagnosed it, with abuse and dependence combined in the oldest survey; dependence on cocaine, cannabis, alcohol or cigarettes, drug by drug; narcotic dependence or addiction in Vietnam, self-reported or by the study's own criteria; DSM-IV alcohol dependence; substance use disorders as each cohort diagnosed them; alcohol problems as each study defined them), with or without treatment as each study defined it
lines.comparator: None (descriptive); the same people's earlier status; in the alcohol review, three different denominators (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, people already recovered)
lines.outcome: No longer meeting the criteria for the problem (remission) at a later interview or at the last follow-up, as each study defined it (not meeting dependence criteria in the past year, meaning two or fewer dependence symptoms, or no symptoms in the oldest survey; time from the start of dependence to remission, drug by drug; not dependent again within about a year, and not addicted again within 3 years, in the Vietnam veterans; not meeting full DSM-IV criteria in the year before an interview about three years later; at least six months without meeting criteria; abstinence or moderate drinking), and the share of it without treatment
lines.magnitude: Heyman (2013), share of lifetime drug dependence not current in the past year, from published lifetime and 12-month prevalences (no intervals): ECA 1980–84 57% (abuse and/or dependence; remission = no symptoms), NCS 1990–92 76%, NCS-R 2001–03 83%, NESARC 2001–02 81% (dependence; remission = two or fewer symptoms). NESARC curves from the onset of dependence, drug by drug: half remitted by about year 4 (cocaine), 6 (cannabis; year 7 on p. 48), 16 (alcohol) and about 30 (cigarettes); two-thirds by year 7 (cocaine), 27 (alcohol), 49 (cigarettes); at 10 years 79%, 69%, 40%, 20% and at 15 years 89%, 81%, 49%, 28% (cocaine, cannabis, alcohol, nicotine); dependent for at least 16 and 23 years 10% and 5% (cocaine), at least 23 and 36 years 10% and 5% (cannabis). Treatment: ECA at most 30% had mentioned drug use to a health specialist; NESARC no more than 16% of current cases in treatment. People in jails and prisons missed: remission about 80% falls to about 64% with a quarter more cases none of whom remitted (about 74% if half of them had stopped by about age 37). Robins (1993), men addicted in Vietnam: addicted again in the first year after return 5%, at any time in 3 years 12%; simple detoxification in service for a third; drug treatment after return entered by under 2% of men who used narcotics in Vietnam, 6% of men positive at departure and 14% of those positive at departure who kept using; two-thirds of treated men relapsed by the time of interview. Robins et al. (1975), general sample N=451, before / in / since Vietnam: narcotic use 11% / 43% / 10%; dependence self-reported 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%, by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%. Still dependent at departure (both samples pooled, no weighting stated, n=134): 50% used narcotics after return, 14% dependent again. A period of more-than-weekly narcotic use since return 3% vs under 0.5% before service. Men first dependent in Vietnam dependent again 8–10 months after return (Figure, approximate): about 2% (general sample, N=90) and about 7% (urine-positive sample, N=341). Stated remission rate 95% (no denominator). Vergés et al. (2012), NESARC 2001–2002 to 2004–2005: 422 of 1,172 with past-year alcohol dependence (36%) dependent again about three years later, about 64% (750) not (1,172 = 422 + 750, and both shares are editors' calculations, unweighted); weighted persistence 32.4% (ages 21–23) and 44.5% (43–52). Fleury et al. (2016), 21 studies (20 cohorts, follow-up 3–50 years, and one lifetime survey estimate entered as 95.7%): standard remission 54.4% (95% CI 42.1–66.2), studies 19.6–95.7%, I² 99.4%; conservative 35.0% (25.2–46.4), I² 99.5%; without the lifetime survey, standard about 50.1% (42.5–57.6; editors' recalculation from Fig. 4, matching the lowest printed leave-one-out value) and conservative 30.9% (26.1–36.1, printed); treatment at baseline 51.1% vs not 62.4% (standard rate, p 0.421; about 48–49% for the five cohorts without treatment at baseline other than the lifetime survey, editors' recalculation; the printed conservative-rate subgroups could not be rebuilt from Fig. 4); standard rate higher with longer follow-up (B 0.046 per year, p 0.004) and lower retention (p 0.016), neither for the conservative rate. Mellor et al. (2019), alcohol, 124 estimates (71 calculated by the reviewers): 2.7% to 98.3%; nine studies with all three methods: all people with a problem 2.7–63.6%, untreated people 6.5–77.9%, remitted people 4.3–94.2% (6.4% with Table 3's values) (unweighted medians 12.4, 38.9 and 43.9, not rates); 78% of remitted people untreated (two Canadian surveys; abstinence or moderate drinking; 56.0% and 65.7% with abstinence only); 12.4% vs 32.6% of untreated people remitted (abstinence vs abstinence or moderate drinking; NESARC); 78% vs 40% of people untreated for three years in remission (any vs moderate or severe disorder; Netherlands); 36.0% vs 14.0% (remission at both 1 and 3 years vs also at 16 years; the 14.0% a reviewers' calculation; a US cohort).
lines.reasoning: Descriptive claim: starts low and is rated as a description of the samples. Down one for risk of bias, because the part of the question about recovery without treatment rests on second-hand, unappraised estimates (and on a meta-analysis of unappraised, mostly treatment-recruited cohorts), and the survey figures for drugs are a reviewer's recalculations: very low. A lenient reading would rate the Vietnam and national-survey figures alone (primary data from a near-complete random sample and weighted national surveys) as low for the narrower statement that many people no longer meet the criteria within one to three years; the rating is set by the weakest necessary link. Not upgraded (descriptive). Status replicated: the direction holds in independent samples (the Vietnam veterans; the US national surveys; the cohorts pooled by Fleury et al.), but the 2001–02 US survey (NESARC) appears in several places: Heyman's survey figure and his curves by drug, which come from the same remission analysis (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011, in Addiction) that Fleury et al. pooled as their lifetime estimate; Vergés et al.; Moss et al. (2010), a general-population sample from the same survey followed for three years, in Fleury et al.; and Dawson et al. in Mellor et al.; these are not counted as independent of each other, and the Vietnam cohort's 1975 report and 1993 lecture are one study. Not used: Heyman's comparison of treated and untreated Vietnam veterans, which joins figures for different groups and time spans; his conclusions that remission does not require treatment and that most people stop by about age 30, which go beyond what the surveys measured; the 95% remission rate as a figure (no stated denominator), Fleury et al.'s annual remission rates (inconsistent with its pooled proportions), its 14 years of use before remission (not derivable from its table) and its conservative-rate comparison by treatment at entry (not reproducible from its study values), and Mellor et al.'s medians as rates (card reporting issues). The comparison of cohorts by treatment at entry describes who entered each study, not who recovered without treatment, and the low share of people in treatment in the surveys describes current cases, not who recovered without it.

lines.q: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment?
lines.short: Many do. In US surveys, about 8 in 10 people who had ever been dependent on a drug no longer counted as dependent in the past year. Treatment was uncommon.
lines.but: That's not the same as quitting. And only alcohol studies counted who got better without treatment.
how: In three US surveys from 1990 to 2003, 76 to 83 in 100 people who had ever been dependent on a drug no longer counted as dependent in the past year. They could still use drugs, or relapse later.

Counted one drug at a time, half of people dependent on cocaine had recovered within about 4 years of becoming dependent, cannabis 6, alcohol 16 and cigarettes 30. Some stayed dependent for decades. Heroin wasn't in these figures.
Of US soldiers addicted to narcotics in Vietnam, 5 in 100 were addicted again in their first year home and 12 in 100 within 3 years. Few entered drug treatment back home.

In 21 long studies, mostly of people found through treatment, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen. For alcohol, counts of recovery without treatment run from about 3 to 98 in 100. That's mostly because studies count different groups.

lines.statement: As described in one narrative review of reports up to 2014 (Wood et al., 2015), so that its figures are second-hand and come from published case reports and case series (several known only from conference abstracts), one US poison-centre series, cases and deaths reported to European agencies and a news report, none of them appraised: NBOMes (N-2-methoxybenzyl relatives of the 2C phenethylamines, among them 25I-, 25B- and 25C-NBOMe; the review describes 25I-NBOMe as a very potent agonist of the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor) were typically sold on blotters, and also as powder and liquid, and 8 of the 10 first detections of an NBOMe in Europe, from January 2011 to June 2013, were on blotters, alone or with powder (editors' count from the review's table). In several reported cases people believed they had taken LSD: a woman at a US festival had taken 'acid' on blotters whose remains held mainly 25C-NBOMe (her own samples were not tested); three people in Belgium who said they had taken 'synthetic LSD' had 25I-NBOMe, and no other drug, in their urine; and among the deaths, a 21-year-old man in Houston who had taken two 'hits of acid' had 25I-NBOMe, with cannabis metabolites, in post-mortem samples, a person in Belgium had used a blotter they thought held LSD, in which no LSD was found (whether an NBOMe was tested for is not reported), and in Richmond, Virginia, a 19-year-old died while 'trip sitting' friends who were using 'acid' blotters, and an unused blotter from the case held 25I-NBOMe, which was also found in his own samples. How often blotters sold as LSD hold an NBOMe was not measured. In the 29 published poisoning cases (25I-NBOMe 23, 25B-NBOMe 3, 25C-NBOMe 3; aged 14 to 31, and 17 of the 19 whose sex is given were men, editors' count), the review reports a fast heart rate in 96.6%, high blood pressure in 62.0%, agitation or aggression in 48.2%, seizures in 37.9% and a high body temperature in 27.6%, and acute kidney injury in 5 people; these features are not defined, and the review's own case descriptions do not reproduce all of the shares (by the editors' count, seizures in 12 of the 29 and kidney injury in 6), so they are approximate. The severe courses described include continuous seizures (status epilepticus), muscle breakdown with kidney injury treated with dialysis or blood filtration in 3 people, lung injury needing a long period on a ventilator, and 38 days in intensive care for a man who injected a liquid labelled 25I-NBOMe (he left hospital after 43 days with normal kidney function); five of seven men in one English series went home from the emergency department within a day. Published cases favour severe ones: in 25 cases reported to Texas poison centres in 2012–2013 (no other substance reported in 21), seizures were recorded in 4% (1 of 25, editors' calculation), against 38% across the published cases, and the commonest effects were a fast heart rate (52%), agitation or irritability (48%), hallucinations (32%) and high blood pressure (32%). Eight deaths had been reported with 25I-NBOMe (in one with 25C-NBOMe too), and the review's abstract says it was detected in all eight, but its text reports laboratory detection in five (two in Houston, one in Richmond, one in Belgium whose death was reported as due to natural causes, and one in the UK, a 22-year-old man who drowned, with 25C-NBOMe and five other substances also found) and none reported for three (an Australian news report, the Belgian death after a blotter thought to hold LSD, and a Polish death). Several deaths followed disturbed behaviour, such as falls from balconies, or self-injury and aggression before collapse, and the review says the role of NBOMes in the deaths had often not been determined. By the editors' count, the NBOMe was found in the person's own samples in 15 of the 29 published poisoning cases, only in the remaining product in 2, and in no sample linked to the person in 12, and other drugs were found or reported in many cases; the review's authors read the reported features as serotonin toxicity together with stimulant-like (sympathomimetic) toxicity, much like MDMA, some amphetamines and mephedrone. These reports count no one who used an NBOMe without harm, so they cannot give the risk of harm from a use, and no source here compares NBOMes with LSD; in two non-representative 2013 surveys aimed at people who go clubbing (one of them by two of the review's authors), NBOMe use was much less common than LSD or mephedrone use (ever used: 2.6% against 39.4% for LSD among 22,289 respondents of the Global Drugs Survey). Nothing after 2014 is covered. How often people seek emergency treatment after taking LSD is a separate answer. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People with reported poisoning or death after NBOMe use, 2010–2014, as gathered in one narrative review: 29 published poisoning cases (several known only from conference abstracts), 25 cases reported to Texas poison centres in 2012–2013, 25 non-fatal cases reported to the EU Early Warning System, and 8 reported deaths (forensic reports, the EU Early Warning System and a news report); first detections of NBOMes in Europe, 2011–2013
lines.exposure: NBOMe drugs (mostly 25I-NBOMe; also 25B- and 25C-NBOMe), reported by the person or found by laboratory analysis of the person's samples or of the product, often with other drugs; the forms in which they were found or taken (blotters, powder, liquid, capsules), including blotters taken as LSD or 'acid'
lines.comparator: None: case reports and one poison-centre series with no comparison group; the review sets the published cases beside the poison-centre series; no comparison with LSD
lines.outcome: Clinical features, severe complications and deaths as reported, whether the drug was confirmed by laboratory analysis, and cases in which people believed they had taken LSD
lines.magnitude: Wood et al. (2015), second-hand: first detections in Europe 2011–2013, 8 of 10 on blotters (editors' count, Table 1). 29 published poisoning cases (25I 23, 25B 3, 25C 3): tachycardia 96.6%, hypertension 62.0%, agitation/aggression 48.2%, seizures 37.9%, hyperthermia 27.6%, acute kidney injury 5 patients (as printed; editors' count from the case descriptions: seizures 12 of 29, kidney injury 6); NBOMe found in the person's own samples in 15 of 29, product only 2, no linked analysis 12 (editors' count). Texas poison centres 2012–2013, 25 cases: tachycardia 52%, agitation/irritability 48%, hallucinations 32%, hypertension 32%, confusion 24%, mydriasis 20%, seizures 4% (1 of 25, editors' calculation) against 38% in published cases. Deaths: 8 reported with 25I-NBOMe (abstract: detected in all 8); laboratory detection in 5, none reported for 3. Global Drugs Survey 2013 (22,289; non-representative): ever used an NBOMe 2.6%, LSD 39.4%. No denominators of people who used NBOMes; no rates or intervals.
lines.reasoning: Descriptive (what was reported, and in which kind of data): starts low as case reports and record series seen through a narrative review; downgraded one level for risk of bias (selected, partly unconfirmed cases, often with other drugs) and one for indirectness (second-hand), bounded at very low; never upgraded. Because every supporting anchor cites one narrative review, the claim stays a draft and its statement says that its figures are second-hand. Status single study: one review; the primary reports it gathers come from different teams but were not read here, so they are not counted as independent replications. The statement gives the review's printed shares, not the editors' recount, and says that they are approximate; it reports deaths with the drug found or reported, not deaths caused by it. Nothing here measures how often blotters sold as LSD hold an NBOMe, the risk of harm from a use, or harm compared with LSD.

lines.q: What are NBOMes, and are they sold as LSD?
lines.short: Yes, sometimes. NBOMes are lab-made drugs, mostly sold on blotters. In case reports up to 2014, several people who got sick or died thought they'd taken LSD.
lines.but: Nobody has counted how often 'LSD' blotters hold NBOMes. And these are reports of people who got sick, so they can't say how risky one use is.
how: NBOMes are lab-made relatives of the 2C drugs. Of the first 10 found in Europe, from 2011 to 2013, 8 were on blotters. In some cases, blotters taken as 'acid' turned out to hold an NBOMe.
In 29 published cases of poisoning, nearly all had a racing heart and about 4 in 10 had seizures. Some needed intensive care, a breathing machine or dialysis.
Published cases are often the worst ones. Of 25 cases reported to Texas poison centres, 4 in 100 had seizures, against about 38 in 100 published cases.
By 2014, eight deaths had been reported with 25I-NBOMe, and a lab found it in five. Some had taken other drugs too. The review says its role in the deaths was often unclear.

lines.statement: Among US civilian adults living in households in 2015 and 2016, past-year misuse of benzodiazepines (any use other than as a doctor directed, by self-report) was reported by 2.2% (95% CI 2.0 to 2.3), against 10.4% (10.1 to 10.7) who reported using them only as prescribed; the people reporting misuse most often gave relaxing or relieving tension (47.1%) or help with sleep (26.6%) as their main reason, and getting high less often (11.6%), and most often got the pills from a friend or relative (68.8% in all, editors' sum). Certainty: low. Status: single study. The figures come from the National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), a national probability survey answered by computer, partly in a private audio-assisted section meant to encourage honest answers, in 86,186 adults (Maust et al., 2019). In all, 12.6% (12.2 to 12.9) reported past-year benzodiazepine use, an estimated 30.6 million adults a year, so misuse made up 17.2% of use (5.3 million people against 25.3 million). Misuse counted taking a benzodiazepine without a prescription and taking one's own in greater amounts, more often or for longer than prescribed, and anyone reporting any misuse in the past year counted as misusing even if they also took it as prescribed. It was most common at ages 18 to 25 (5.2% of all adults that age; 51.0% of their benzodiazepine use) and least common at 65 or older (0.6%). Of the 2,533 people reporting misuse, 73.9% had taken a benzodiazepine without a prescription; the one misused was most often alprazolam (Xanax; 75.1%), then diazepam (20.5%), clonazepam (20.0%) and lorazepam (15.4%), some people naming more than one. Their main reasons, from a list: to relax or relieve tension 47.1%, to help with sleep 26.6%, to get high 11.6%, to help with feelings or emotions 10.1%, to experiment 6.0%, to increase or decrease the effects of another drug 1.6%, and 'hooked or have to have it' 0.6%. These shares add to 103.6% (editors' sum; 104.0% at ages 18 to 49 and 101.3% at 50 or older), more than rounding can explain, and 'another reason', also on the list, is not shown; the paper does not say whether people could give more than one main reason, so the shares cannot be read as exactly one reason per person. Getting high was the main reason for 13.9% at ages 18 to 49 and 3.0% at 50 or older, and sleep for 22.4% and 41.7%. Sources: free from a friend or relative 53.2%, bought from one 12.3% and stolen from one 3.3%, one doctor 19.5%, two or more doctors 0.9%, bought from a dealer or stranger 7.7%, and stolen from a health care setting 0.1% (together 97.0%, editors' sum; the rest not shown). Of the people reporting misuse, 4.6% (3.7 to 5.6) met DSM-IV criteria for past-year abuse and 6.8% (5.6 to 8.2) for past-year dependence, and they reported a mean of 5.4 days of misuse in the past month (whether people with no misuse that month are counted is not stated). Among people who used benzodiazepines, misuse rather than use as prescribed went with younger age, being male, and use, misuse or use disorders of alcohol, marijuana, prescription opioids and prescription stimulants, a cross-sectional association that shows nothing about cause. All of it is self-report without checks; adults in institutions and on active military duty are not covered; response rates are not given; and the 2015 redesign of the survey means the figures cannot be compared with earlier years. The authors suggest that part of what the survey counts as misuse may be people treating anxiety or insomnia that has gone untreated because of poor access to care; the analysis did not test this.
lines.population: US civilian adults aged 18 or older living in households, National Survey on Drug Use and Health 2015 and 2016 (86,186 respondents; 10,290 reporting past-year benzodiazepine use; 2,533 reporting misuse, 2,357 of them aged 18 to 49 and 176 aged 50 or older); people in institutions and on active military duty not covered
lines.exposure: Self-reported past-year benzodiazepine use, only as prescribed or with misuse (any use other than as a doctor directed: without a prescription, or in greater amounts, more often or longer than prescribed), reported in the survey's tranquilizer and sedative sections
lines.comparator: None for the shares among people reporting misuse (descriptive); use only as prescribed, for the share of use that was misuse and for the factors that went with misuse; ages 18 to 49 against 50 or older
lines.outcome: Self-reported past-year use and misuse; among people reporting misuse, its type, main reason (from a list), source and the benzodiazepine misused; days of misuse in the past month; DSM-IV abuse and dependence
lines.magnitude: Maust et al. (2019), NSDUH 2015–2016, survey-weighted: past-year any use 12.6% (95% CI 12.2–12.9), 30.6 million adults a year (29.7–31.5 million); only as prescribed 10.4% (10.1–10.7), 25.3 million (24.5–26.1); misuse 2.2% (2.0–2.3), 5.3 million (5.0–5.6); misuse 17.2% of use. Misuse by age, all adults: 18–25 5.2% (4.8–5.6), 26–34 3.3%, 35–49 1.7%, 50–64 1.4%, 65 or older 0.6% (0.4–0.8); as a share of use 51.0%, 28.6%, 13.8%, 9.7% and 4.4%. Among 2,533 reporting misuse (Table 3): without a prescription 73.9%, in greater amounts 16.0%, more often 10.1%, longer 4.9%, other ways 18.7%. Source: free from a friend or relative 53.2%, bought from one 12.3%, stolen from one 3.3% (68.8%, editors' sum), one clinician 19.5%, two or more clinicians 0.9%, bought from a dealer or stranger 7.7%, stolen from a health care setting 0.1% (97.0% in all, editors' sum). Medication misused: alprazolam 75.1%, diazepam 20.5%, clonazepam 20.0%, lorazepam 15.4%. DSM-IV past-year abuse 4.6% (3.7–5.6), dependence 6.8% (5.6–8.2); mean days of misuse in the past month 5.4 (SE 0.3). Misuse against use as prescribed, adjusted OR: 65 or older against 18–25 0.23 (0.15–0.34); women 0.74 (0.61–0.90); alcohol abuse or dependence 2.31 (1.73–3.09); marijuana abuse or dependence 2.39 (1.62–3.52); prescription opioid misuse 4.11 (3.26–5.18), abuse or dependence 4.81 (3.45–6.72), use as prescribed 0.69 (0.57–0.84); prescription stimulant misuse 2.46 (1.85–3.27), abuse or dependence 3.40 (1.72–6.70), use as prescribed 0.90 (0.74–1.09).
lines.reasoning: Descriptive (prevalence, and self-reported reasons and sources, in a national survey): starts low and is never upgraded; not downgraded (see the domain notes). The reasons are people's own answers to a list and are worded as such; their printed shares add to 103.6%, which the statement says, so they cannot be read as exactly one reason per person, but the order (relaxing, then sleep, then getting high) does not depend on the extra 3.6 points. The associations with other substances are cross-sectional and show nothing about cause. The authors' suggestion that some misuse reflects poor access to care is given as their untested suggestion. The abstract's advice to monitor patients also prescribed opioids or stimulants is left out, because the paper's own Table 2 does not support it (prescribed opioid use went with lower odds of misuse, prescribed stimulant use with no difference). Status single study: one analysis of one survey's first two years after its redesign.

lines.q: Why do people misuse Xanax and other benzos?
lines.short: Mostly to relax or sleep, they say. In a big US survey, 47 in 100 people who misused benzos named relaxing as the main reason, 27 sleep, and 12 getting high.
lines.but: It's what people told a survey. And 'misuse' here also counts taking more of your own pills than your doctor said.
how: In a US survey in 2015 and 2016, about 13 in 100 adults had used a benzo in the past year. About 2 in 100 had misused one. At ages 18 to 25, about half of all benzo use was misuse.
Misuse meant any use a doctor didn't direct. Most often (74 in 100) it was pills without a prescription. Three in four had misused alprazolam (Xanax).
Main reasons: relaxing 47 in 100, sleep 27, getting high 12, coping with feelings 10. These add up to a bit over 100, and the paper doesn't say why.
About 69 in 100 got the pills from a friend or relative, mostly for free, and 20 in 100 from one doctor. About 7 in 100 met the criteria for dependence.

lines.statement: In children and adolescents (5 to 17 years) and adults with ADHD in double-blind randomized trials of prescribed medicines, analysed at the time closest to 12 weeks (in the blood-pressure review the trials lasted a median of 7 weeks), amphetamine medicines compared with methylphenidate were associated with a slightly larger reduction in clinician-rated ADHD symptoms, a difference the review itself rates as low certainty and that rests partly on indirect comparisons in children and adolescents and only on indirect comparisons in adults, while stopping a trial because of side effects and the rises in blood pressure and pulse did not differ significantly between the two, without being shown to be equal (Cortese et al., 2018; Farhat et al., 2025). The one blinded trial here that gave children both drugs found about the same number of side-effect complaints on each but rated them somewhat more severe on dexamphetamine, at one fixed dose of each and with no placebo (Efron et al., 1997). Benefit: in a network meta-analysis of 133 double-blind trials to April 2017 (81 in children and adolescents, 51 in adults and 1 in both; 14,346 children and adolescents and 10,296 adults; symptom analyses in 10,068 and 8131), both medicines reduced clinician-rated core symptoms more than placebo, amphetamines by a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 1.02 in children and adolescents and 0.79 in adults and methylphenidate by 0.78 and 0.49 (all four of moderate certainty by the review's GRADE ratings); amphetamines against methylphenidate gave SMDs of −0.24 (95% CI −0.44 to −0.05) in children and adolescents and −0.29 (−0.54 to −0.05) in adults, both of low certainty, an advantage the authors call marginal in children and adolescents. Teachers' ratings were available for methylphenidate (SMD −0.82 against placebo, low certainty) but not for amphetamines, and clinicians' global improvement ratings did not differ significantly between the two (no estimate printed). The abstract calls the symptom differences head-to-head comparisons, but they are network estimates: by the authors' account head-to-head trials were few and comparisons between drugs were frequently based on indirect evidence, and the network plot shows no trial comparing the two in adults. Stopping because of side effects (11,018 children and adolescents and 5362 adults): against placebo, the odds of leaving a trial because of side effects were higher with amphetamines (odds ratio 2.30, 1.36 to 3.89, in children and adolescents; 3.26, 1.54 to 6.92, in adults; moderate certainty) and with methylphenidate in adults (2.39, 1.40 to 4.08, high certainty), but not clearly with methylphenidate in children and adolescents (1.44, 0.90 to 2.31, low certainty); amphetamines against methylphenidate gave 1.60 (0.94 to 2.73, low certainty) in children and adolescents and 1.36 (0.54 to 3.43, very low certainty) in adults, neither significant, so more stopping on amphetamines is neither shown nor ruled out. The article gives odds ratios only, not how many people stopped. The authors' preference for methylphenidate in children and adolescents and amphetamines in adults rests on each drug's comparison with placebo (in children and adolescents methylphenidate was the only medicine with better acceptability than placebo and, unlike amphetamines, was not worse tolerated than placebo), not on a difference between the two. Both lowered weight against placebo (SMDs −0.71 in children and adolescents and −0.60 in adults with amphetamines, −0.77 and −0.74 with methylphenidate; no comparison of the two is printed). Blood pressure and pulse: in a second network meta-analysis by an overlapping team that reused and extended the first one's searches to January 2024 (102 trials; 13,315 children and adolescents, mean age 11, and 9387 adults, mean age 35; median trial length 7 weeks; 87 of the 102 trials industry funded), the average rises against placebo, which the authors describe as small on average, were: in children and adolescents, systolic pressure +1.81 mm Hg, diastolic +2.42 and pulse +3.88 beats a minute with methylphenidate; +0.87 (not significant), +1.93 and +1.78 (not significant) with amphetamines; and +1.76, +2.29 and +4.17 with lisdexamfetamine, analysed separately; in adults, all of very low certainty, +1.66, +1.6 and +4.37 with methylphenidate, +2.3, +1.91 and +5.18 with amphetamines, and +1.62 (not significant), +3.07 and +5.07 with lisdexamfetamine. Neither amphetamines nor lisdexamfetamine differed significantly from methylphenidate in either age group: amphetamines minus methylphenidate, systolic −0.94 mm Hg (−2.33 to 0.44, high certainty) in children and adolescents and +0.64 (−1.44 to 2.72) in adults, diastolic −0.49 (−1.87 to 0.88) and +0.31 (−1.87 to 2.49) (editors' sign reversal of the printed methylphenidate-minus-amphetamines values), and pulse −2.1 beats a minute (−4.25 to 0.06) and +0.81 (−1.29 to 2.90). All adult trials were placebo-controlled, so every adult comparison between medicines is indirect; restricted to licensed doses, the authors report that only amphetamines or lisdexamfetamine were still consistently associated with higher blood pressure than placebo in adults (numbers only in the appendix, not read); only four trials gave 24-week results and none longer; and these are group averages, which the authors say some people may exceed. The head-to-head trial: 125 children aged 5 to 15 (114 boys) referred to a hospital clinic in Melbourne took dexamphetamine, an amphetamine, and methylphenidate in identical capsules twice a day for two weeks each, in random order, with investigators, families, children and teachers blind to the order. On parents' ratings of 17 listed complaints (0 absent, 1 to 9 for severity; a scale without published norms), the mean number of complaints was 7.64 on dexamphetamine and 7.19 on methylphenidate (not different) against 8.19 before treatment, and the mean severity of the complaints reported was 3.73 against 3.24 (significant; 4.08 before treatment); six items were rated more severe on dexamphetamine (trouble sleeping 3.61 against 2.69, irritability 3.65 against 2.94, proneness to crying 3.4 against 2.7, anxiousness 2.71 against 2.07, sadness or unhappiness 2.43 against 1.69, nightmares 0.79 against 0.48), none on methylphenidate, and two children stopped on each drug because of severe effects. Many complaints were already reported before any medicine (irritability in 102 of the 125 children, anxiousness in 96), and only poor appetite (43 before, 74 on dexamphetamine, 69 on methylphenidate) and trouble sleeping on dexamphetamine (67 before, 88) were more frequent on a drug than before; with no placebo, changes from before treatment cannot be attributed to the drugs. Each drug was given at one fixed dose set by body weight, and the paper does not report whether the two doses worked equally well (parents rated 86 children improved on dexamphetamine and 90 on methylphenidate, not tested), so the difference in severity may reflect the doses chosen. These are prescribed medicines at licensed or guideline doses, studied over weeks in people diagnosed with ADHD; the papers say nothing about long-term use or about use without a prescription. Psychosis, which neither review studied, is a separate answer (see the answer on psychosis after starting amphetamine or methylphenidate). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Children and adolescents aged 5 to 17 and adults with a primary diagnosis of ADHD in double-blind randomized trials of at least 1 week (133 trials to April 2017: 14,346 children and adolescents and 10,296 adults; 102 trials to January 2024: 13,315 children and adolescents, mean age 11, and 9387 adults, mean age 35, mostly from high-income countries; the two sets of trials overlap); and 125 children aged 5 to 15 (114 boys) with DSM-IV ADHD referred to a hospital clinic in Melbourne, 1995–1996

(2018); amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine as separate groups in Farhat et al. (2025); dexamphetamine twice a day for 2 weeks at one fixed weight-based dose (0.15 mg/kg per dose) in Efron et al. (1997)
