Clinician-rated core symptoms, SMD against placebo: amphetamines −1.02 (−1.19 to −0.85) children and adolescents, −0.79 (−0.99 to −0.58) adults; methylphenidate −0.78 (−0.93 to −0.62) and −0.49 (−0.64 to −0.35); all moderate. Amphetamines against methylphenidate −0.24 (−0.44 to −0.05) and −0.29 (−0.54 to −0.05), both low. Teachers' ratings: methylphenidate −0.82 (−1.16 to −0.48, low); no data for amphetamines. CGI-I: amphetamines and methylphenidate not significantly different (no estimate printed). Leaving because of side effects, OR against placebo: amphetamines 2.30 (1.36–3.89) and 3.26 (1.54–6.92), moderate; methylphenidate 1.44 (0.90–2.31, low) and 2.39 (1.40–4.08, high); amphetamines against methylphenidate 1.60 (0.94–2.73, low) and 1.36 (0.54–3.43, very low), values above 1 meaning more leaving on amphetamines. Acceptability against placebo: methylphenidate in children and adolescents 0.69 (0.52–0.91); amphetamines in adults 0.68 (0.49–0.95). Weight, SMD against placebo: amphetamines −0.71 (−1.15 to −0.27) and −0.60 (−1.03 to −0.18); methylphenidate −0.77 (−1.09 to −0.45) and −0.74 (−1.20 to −0.28). Trials 133 (81, 51, 1 both); participants 14,346 and 10,296; symptom analysis 10,068 and 8131; stopping analysis 11,018 and 5362. Farhat et al. (2025), mean difference against placebo at the time closest to 12 weeks (median 7 weeks), CINeMA certainty: children and adolescents, methylphenidate systolic 1.81 mm Hg (1.05 to 2.57, moderate), diastolic 2.42 (1.69 to 3.15, low), pulse 3.88 beats a minute (2.87 to 4.89 in Figure 3; 4.8 in the text and Figure 5; moderate); amphetamines 0.87 (−0.3 to 2.03, high), 1.93 (0.74 to 3.11, high), 1.78 (−0.12 to 3.69, moderate); lisdexamfetamine 1.76 (0.68 to 2.83, moderate), 2.29 (1.25 to 3.34, low), 4.17 (2.74 to 5.61, very low). Adults (all very low): methylphenidate 1.66 (0.38 to 2.93), 1.6 (0.29 to 2.91), 4.37 (3.16 to 5.59); amphetamines 2.3 (0.66 to 3.94), 1.91 (0.17 to 3.65), 5.18 (3.47 to 6.89); lisdexamfetamine 1.62 (−0.81 to 4.06), 3.07 (0.69 to 5.45), 5.07 (2.76 to 7.37). Amphetamines minus methylphenidate: systolic −0.94 (−2.33 to 0.44, high) and 0.64 (−1.44 to 2.72); diastolic as printed (methylphenidate minus amphetamines) 0.49 (−0.88 to 1.87, high) and −0.31 (−2.49 to 1.87); pulse −2.1 (−4.25 to 0.06) and 0.81 (−1.29 to 2.90). Lisdexamfetamine minus methylphenidate: systolic −0.06 (−1.17 to 1.06, moderate) and −0.04 (−2.79 to 2.71); diastolic as printed (methylphenidate minus lisdexamfetamine) 0.13 (−0.98 to 1.24, moderate) and −1.47 (−4.19 to 1.25); pulse 0.29 (−1.24 to 1.83, low) and 0.69 (−1.92 to 3.3). Figure 5 also marks amphetamines minus lisdexamfetamine pulse in children and adolescents as −2.39 (−4.78 to −0.01, low), which the text leaves out. Trials 102 (61 children and adolescents, 13,315 people; 41 adults, 9387); 87 industry funded; four with 24-week data, none longer. Efron et al. (1997), 125 children, parent ratings on 17 items (0 to 9): number of complaints, mean (SD), before 8.19 (3.97), dexamphetamine 7.64 (3.83), methylphenidate 7.19 (3.82), F(2,122) = 3.72, p = .03 (only before against methylphenidate significant at p < .01); mean severity 4.08 (1.56), 3.73 (1.68), 3.24 (1.46), F = 15.98, p < .01 (before against methylphenidate and dexamphetamine against methylphenidate significant). Item severity, before, dexamphetamine, methylphenidate: trouble sleeping 2.21, 3.61, 2.69; poor appetite 1.22, 2.74, 2.12; irritability 4.57, 3.65, 2.94; proneness to crying 3.35, 3.4, 2.7; anxiousness 3.94, 2.71, 2.07; sadness or unhappiness 2.86, 2.43, 1.69; nightmares 1.09, 0.79, 0.48. Counts of 125 before, on dexamphetamine and on methylphenidate: poor appetite 43, 74, 69; trouble sleeping 67, 88, 79; irritability 102, 102, 100; anxiousness 96, 85, 76. Stopped a period because of severe effects: 2 on each drug (4 of 125). Parents' global rating improved: 86 (68.8%) on dexamphetamine, 90 (72%) on methylphenidate, not tested.
lines.reasoning: Randomized trials start high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1, indirectness −1; inconsistency, imprecision and publication bias 0. Low for the statement as worded: in short trials of prescribed medicines in people with ADHD, amphetamines gave a slightly larger reduction in clinician-rated symptoms than methylphenidate (the review's own GRADE: low in both age groups), while stopping because of side effects and rises in blood pressure and pulse were not shown to differ. Taken alone, the adult comparisons and the comparison of stopping would be very low (indirect only, or imprecise; the review rates the adult comparison of stopping very low), and the head-to-head trial's severity finding, one trial at one fixed dose of each drug with parent ratings on a scale without norms, would be low. Relation 'is associated with': the trials were randomized, but the comparison between the two drugs is mostly indirect, which is not a randomized comparison. Status single study: each finding rests on one source (symptoms and stopping on one network meta-analysis; blood pressure and pulse on a second that reused its searches and shares three authors; side-effect severity on one trial), and the trial-by-trial results are in appendices that were not read, so the trials inside the networks are not counted as independent replications here. Not rated: long-term effects, numbers of people who stop, psychosis (a separate answer) and use without a prescription.

lines.q: Adderall or Ritalin: which works better, and which has more side effects?
lines.short: Both work. In a review of 133 short trials, amphetamine (as in Adderall) eased symptoms a bit more than methylphenidate (Ritalin). Neither clearly made more people quit over side effects.
lines.but: Few trials tested the two head to head, and none in adults. Most compared one drug with a dummy pill, for a few weeks.
how: A review pooled 133 trials in about 14,300 children and teens and 10,300 adults. On doctors' ratings after about 12 weeks, amphetamine eased symptoms a little more than methylphenidate. The review rated this low certainty.

Quitting because of side effects wasn't clearly different between the two, but a gap wasn't ruled out. Against a dummy pill, more quit on amphetamine at every age, and on methylphenidate in adults. Both lowered weight.

Over about 7 weeks, blood pressure rose by about 1 to 3 points and heart rate by about 2 to 5 beats a minute on average, compared with a dummy pill. The two drugs didn't clearly differ, in 102 trials.

One blinded trial gave 125 children both, two weeks each, with no dummy pill. Parents counted as many complaints on each, but rated sleep and mood ones a bit worse on dexamphetamine, a kind of amphetamine. Many, like irritability (82 in 100), were there before any medicine.

lines.statement: In 28 healthy, screened adults (14 women, 14 men; mean age 35; half had used a psychedelic before) who each took LSD (100 and 200 µg as labelled, in solution), psilocybin (15 and 30 mg, in capsules of the pure drug, not mushrooms) and a dummy, one per hospital session at least 10 days apart, in random, counterbalanced order under double-blind, double-dummy conditions (study conditions), LSD compared with psilocybin made the effects last longer, and the higher LSD dose raised heart rate more, while the higher psilocybin dose raised blood pressure and body temperature more; ratings of what the experience was like did not differ significantly between the higher psilocybin dose and either LSD dose on almost every scale, which in 28 people does not show that the experiences are the same (Holze et al., 2022). Length: from each person's 'any drug effect' ratings (a modelled curve, counted from and to 10% of the person's own peak), the effects lasted on average 5.6 hours (SD 2.2) after psilocybin 15 mg, 6.5 (2.4) after 30 mg, 9.3 (3.2) after LSD 100 µg and 11 (3.7) after 200 µg (both LSD doses longer than both psilocybin doses, p < 0.001); they began on average 0.4 to 0.6 hours after LSD and 0.8 hours after psilocybin, which the authors put down to LSD being a liquid and psilocybin a capsule, not to the drugs, and they say, without a formal test, that LSD's longer half-life in blood (about 4 hours, against about 2.5 for psilocin, the form psilocybin takes in the body) fully explains the longer duration. Kind: psilocybin 30 mg and either LSD dose did not differ significantly on any visual analogue scale or on any subscale of the main altered-states questionnaire (5D-ASC); LSD 200 µg was rated higher than psilocybin 30 mg only on 'ineffability' (how hard the experience was to put into words), and both LSD doses raised 'emotional excitation' on a mood scale more than psilocybin (one more mood reading, 'dreaminess' at its lowest point, differed for LSD 100 µg); the lower psilocybin dose gave lower peak ratings than the higher one on several scales. These are non-significant post hoc tests without equivalence margins (Supplementary Tables S1–S4), so the abstract's conclusion that the two drugs' effects do not differ beyond duration goes further than the tests can. Body: both drugs raised blood pressure, body temperature and pupil size against the dummy; psilocybin 30 mg raised blood pressure and body temperature significantly more than either LSD dose; LSD 200 µg raised heart rate more than both psilocybin doses, while LSD 100 µg did not differ significantly from either (Supplementary Table S5; the results text says both LSD doses did, which the table contradicts for 100 µg). The differences were modest: averaging each person's highest reading, systolic pressure peaked at 146 mmHg after psilocybin 30 mg, 140 after psilocybin 15 mg, 138 and 141 after LSD 100 and 200 µg, and 131 on the dummy; heart rate at 82 and 78 beats a minute after psilocybin 30 and 15 mg, 83 and 90 after LSD 100 and 200 µg, and 74 on the dummy; body temperature at 37.9 °C after psilocybin 30 mg, 37.5 to 37.6 after the other active conditions and 37.1 on the dummy. Unwanted effects: total scores on a list of complaints in the first 12 hours rose with all four active conditions against the dummy, with no significant difference between the higher doses of the two drugs, and from 12 to 24 hours with the higher dose of each drug; on that list, a headache in the first 12 hours was reported by 14 and 18 of the 28 after psilocybin 15 and 30 mg and by 13 after each LSD dose, against 8 on the dummy (no tests of these counts); among events people reported on their own in the evening or within 48 hours, counted by drug, 4 people had a headache after psilocybin and 3 after LSD, 2 had low mood after each, 2 and 1 had nausea, and there was one migraine (LSD) and one nosebleed (psilocybin), with 9 flashback episodes in 5 people within 72 hours (5 after LSD, 4 after psilocybin; what was counted is not explained) and no severe adverse event. Blinding: the dummy was named correctly after every session (100%; 96% when people were asked again at the end of the study), and although the paper says no clear distinction between LSD and psilocybin could be made, people named the right drug (either dose) after 71% of psilocybin 15 mg sessions, 86% of psilocybin 30 mg sessions, 78% of LSD 100 µg sessions and 79% of LSD 200 µg sessions (editors' calculation from Supplementary Table S8: correct guesses plus guesses of the other dose of the same drug), so expectation may have shaped the ratings. How strongly people felt each condition varied widely from person to person (ranges in Table 1), and nobody took a second dose, so taking more was not tested. The study did not test which amounts of the two drugs match, and this answer gives none; the authors' figures on matching amounts rest on doses this study did not give. Two printed means for LSD 100 µg in Table 1 lie outside their own ranges, and the pharmacokinetics paragraph misprints a range (1.75 to 3.0 hours where Supplementary Table S7 gives 0.75 to 3.0). The volunteers had little drug experience (at most 10 lifetime uses of illicit drugs other than cannabis) and no personal or family history of major psychiatric illness, and were in a calm hospital room with an investigator; the LSD solution held about 15% less than its label (84.5 µg per 100 µg unit). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
lines.population: 28 healthy, screened adults (14 women, 14 men; mean age 35, range 25 to 52), recruited by word of mouth or from a pool of people interested in psychedelic trials, and paid; 14 had used a psychedelic before and 10 had never used an illicit drug other than cannabis; excluded were a personal or first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder, interfering medicines and more than 10 lifetime uses of illicit drugs (cannabis excepted); Basel
lines.exposure: Single oral doses of LSD base as a solution, labelled 100 and 200 µg (analysed content 84.5 µg per 100 µg unit), given double-blind and double-dummy in a calm hospital room with one investigator, in random, counterbalanced order with at least 10 days between sessions (study conditions)
lines.comparator: Psilocybin 15 and 30 mg in capsules (analysed 4.61 mg per 5 mg capsule) and placebo, in the same people on other days
lines.outcome: Duration and onset of self-rated effects (modelled from 'any drug effect' ratings); peak self-ratings on visual analogue scales, the 5D-ASC (primary outcome, rated at 24 hours), mystical-experience and mood scales; blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and pupil size; complaint scores for 0 to 12 and 12 to 24 hours and adverse events within 48 to 72 hours; guesses of which drug was given
lines.magnitude: Holze et al. (2022), 28 people. Table 1 (mean ± SD, range; psilocybin 15 mg, psilocybin 30 mg, LSD 100 µg, LSD 200 µg): effect duration 5.6 ± 2.2 (2.5–10), 6.5 ± 2.4 (3.7–12), 9.3 ± 3.2 (5.7–17) and 11 ± 3.7 (5.4–20) h, F(3,81) = 34.4, p < 0.001, both LSD doses longer than both psilocybin doses (p < 0.001); time to onset 0.8 ± 0.3, 0.8 ± 0.4, 0.6 ± 0.2 and 0.4 ± 0.2 h, F(3,81) = 12.5 (LSD 100 µg different only from psilocybin 30 mg, p < 0.05; LSD 200 µg from both, p < 0.001). Supplementary Tables S1–S8 (mean ± SEM unless stated; placebo, psilocybin 15 mg, psilocybin 30 mg, LSD 100 µg, LSD 200 µg; N = 28, F(4,108), Tukey tests, no correction across outcomes). Peak subjective effects: psilocybin 30 mg against either LSD dose, no significant difference on any of the 30 visual analogue rows (any drug effect 88 ± 3.3 against 85 ± 3.2 and 95 ± 2.1% of maximum) or the 18 5D-ASC rows (total score 29 ± 2.3 against 27 ± 2.9 and 35 ± 2.9%) (Tables S1, S3); against LSD 200 µg only MEQ ineffability differed (MEQ30 p < 0.05, MEQ43 p < 0.01; Table S2); AMRS emotional excitation (peak change from baseline) −0.9 ± 0.4, 2.5 ± 0.6, 3.2 ± 0.8, 6.5 ± 1.1 and 6.1 ± 0.9 (psilocybin 30 mg below LSD 100 µg, p < 0.01, and LSD 200 µg, p < 0.05), and AMRS dreaminess (lowest change) −0.1 ± 0.2 after psilocybin 30 mg against 1.1 ± 0.4 after LSD 100 µg (p < 0.05) (Table S4). Autonomic (Table S5, average of each person's highest value): systolic 131 ± 2.0, 140 ± 2.2, 146 ± 2.7, 138 ± 2.4 and 141 ± 2.5 mmHg (psilocybin 30 mg above LSD 100 µg, p < 0.001, and LSD 200 µg, p < 0.05); diastolic 82 ± 1.1, 89 ± 1.6, 93 ± 1.6, 86 ± 1.6 and 87 ± 1.7 (psilocybin 30 mg above both LSD doses, p < 0.001); heart rate 74 ± 2.0, 78 ± 2.1, 82 ± 3.1, 83 ± 2.5 and 90 ± 3.2 beats/min, F = 14.8 (LSD 200 µg above psilocybin 15 mg, p < 0.001, psilocybin 30 mg, p < 0.01, and LSD 100 µg, p < 0.05; LSD 100 µg against either psilocybin dose not significant; psilocybin 15 mg against placebo not significant); body temperature 37.1 ± 0.1, 37.6 ± 0.07, 37.9 ± 0.09, 37.6 ± 0.05 and 37.5 ± 0.08 °C (psilocybin 30 mg above both LSD doses, p < 0.01); rate-pressure product 9334, 10443, 11344, 11119 and 12097 mmHg × beats/min (psilocybin 30 mg against either LSD dose not significant). Editors' calculation, each active condition's peak above the dummy's (psilocybin 15 mg, 30 mg, LSD 100 µg, 200 µg): systolic 9, 15, 7 and 10 mmHg; heart rate 4, 8, 9 and 16 beats/min; temperature 0.5, 0.8, 0.5 and 0.4 °C. The results text (p. 1182) says both LSD doses raised heart rate more than both psilocybin doses; Table S5 shows this only for 200 µg. Complaints (Table S5, total scores): acute (0–12 h) 1.9 ± 0.6, 8.9 ± 1.4, 13 ± 1.6, 12 ± 2.0 and 15 ± 2.0 (all four above placebo, p < 0.001; psilocybin 15 mg below LSD 200 µg, p < 0.01; psilocybin 30 mg against LSD 200 µg not significant); subacute (12–24 h) 1.3 ± 0.3, 2.4 ± 0.5, 4.1 ± 0.8, 3.1 ± 0.6 and 4.8 ± 0.8 (above placebo only psilocybin 30 mg, p < 0.01, and LSD 200 µg, p < 0.001). Headache on the checklist, number of the 28 (Table S6; no tests): 8, 14, 18, 13 and 13 in 0–12 h and 6, 10, 14, 8 and 10 in 12–24 h, with 1, 1, 0, 2 and 2 reporting one before the dose. Events reported by people themselves within 48 h, by drug (psilocybin, LSD; article p. 1183): headache 4 and 3; migraine 0 and 1; nosebleed 1 and 0; low mood 2 and 2; nausea 2 and 1; nightmares 1 and 0; restlessness 1 and 1; vivid dreams 0 and 1; insomnia 1 and 0; involuntary leg movements 0 and 1; flashbacks 9 episodes in 5 people within 72 h (4 after psilocybin, 5 after LSD); no severe adverse events. Half-lives (geometric mean, range; Table S7): LSD 4.3 (2.5–6.0) and 4.0 (2.3–7.1) h; psilocin 2.4 (1.7–3.1) and 2.7 (1.9–3.4) h; LSD 100 µg time to peak concentration 1.6 h, range 0.75–3.0 (the article prints 1.75–3.0). Blinding (Table S8, after each session / at the end of the study, % of 28): placebo named correctly 100 / 96; the given condition named correctly 64 / 75, 57 / 57, 57 / 61 and 61 / 68 (psilocybin 15 mg, 30 mg, LSD 100 µg, 200 µg); the right drug, either dose, after the session 71, 86, 78 and 79 (editors' calculation: 64 + 7, 57 + 29, 57 + 21 and 61 + 18; as people, about 20, 24, 22 and 22 of 28) and at the end of the study 96, 64, 75 and 86 (75 + 21, 57 + 7, 61 + 14 and 68 + 18).
lines.reasoning: Randomized, counterbalanced within-person comparison: starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias −1 (self-ratings under weak blinding between the two drugs, a results text that contradicts its own supplementary table, misprinted values) and imprecision −1 (28 people; sameness in kind cannot be shown without equivalence testing) give low. The duration difference on its own (about 9 to 11 hours against 6 to 7, in the same people, with a decisive test and a plausible link to the half-lives) would be rated moderate, held down only by the self-rated outcome; the statement that the experiences were alike in kind would be rated low or lower, and is worded as not shown either way. Status single study: the first within-person comparison, from one laboratory. The authors' dose-equivalence figures rest on doses not given in this study and are not used; no comparison of strength is made. The online supplement, read in round pdf-2026-11-26, gives the peak values, the guesses and the complaint counts; it does not change the rating.

lines.q: LSD or mushrooms: what's actually different?
lines.short: Mostly how long it lasts: about 9 to 11 hours for LSD, 6 to 7 for psilocybin, the drug in mushrooms. Otherwise 28 lab volunteers rated the trips alike on most measures.
lines.but: Finding no difference in 28 people doesn't prove there is none. And most could tell which drug they'd had.
how: 28 healthy adults each had five hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got a dummy, two amounts of LSD and two of psilocybin, in random order, not told which.
LSD lasted longer at both amounts. It also began a bit sooner, which the authors put down to it being a liquid, not a capsule.

The higher psilocybin amount raised blood pressure and body temperature a little more; the higher LSD amount raised heart rate more. On a checklist, 13 to 18 of the 28 had a headache in the first 12 hours after the drugs, against 8 on the dummy. Nobody had a serious problem.
People named the right drug after 71 to 86 in 100 sessions, and the dummy after every session, which may have shaped their ratings. It used pure psilocybin in capsules, not mushrooms.

lines.statement: As described in a narrative review by the researchers who ran the studies it summarizes (Greenwald et al., 2014, read from the corrected proof), so that every figure here is second-hand, daily buprenorphine under the tongue, compared with placebo, went with fewer of the brain's µ-opioid receptors free to bind a tracer in PET scans, falling as the dose rose, in people dependent on heroin who were not in treatment; responses to heroin and to hydromorphone, another opioid, were reduced but not abolished at the doses studied; and after a daily 16 mg was stopped, the share of free receptors rose over the three days measured. The authors speak of 'availability' (the share of receptors free) rather than 'occupancy', which cannot be measured directly in people; a fall in availability equals a rise in occupancy only if receptor affinity and the body's own opioids stay constant. Scans began 4 hours after the daily dose, the earliest time studied, which the authors say probably misses the largest fall. In 3 men given 2 mg, then 16 mg, then placebo, double blind (Zubieta et al., 2000), availability against placebo ranged across brain regions from 50% to 64% at 2 mg a day and from 5% to 21% at 16 mg, and withdrawal and heroin-craving scores fell as the dose rose. In 5 volunteers given 32, 16, 2 and 0 mg a day for 12 days each (Greenwald et al., 2003), the regional means were 53% to 72% at 2 mg, 9% to 20% at 16 mg and 2% to 12% at 32 mg; urine tests showed that they kept using opioids between inpatient stays, even at 32 mg a day. In 7 volunteers taking buprenorphine with naloxone (2/0.5, 8/2 and 32/8 mg a day, 14 days each) and tested 15 hours after the dose, against a separate group of 8 on placebo (Comer et al., 2005), self-administration of the larger heroin doses offered decreased only modestly at each maintenance dose, when receptor availability, estimated by a model from behaviour rather than imaged, was 21%, 11% and 6%; the authors' re-analysis suggests that nearly all receptors would have to be occupied, beyond what 32 mg a day achieved, to suppress heroin self-administration fully, and in another of their studies 16 mg a day, or 32 mg every other day, did not fully block the reinforcing effect of injected hydromorphone (Greenwald et al., 2002). The review mentions people who try to get past the block with larger amounts of other opioids, but it reports no data on what happens when they do. In 10 volunteers stabilized on 16 mg a day and then switched, double blind, to placebo (Greenwald et al., 2007), scans 4, 28, 52 and 76 hours after the last dose gave availability of 27% to 31%, 54% to 61%, 65% to 75% and 77% to 94%, against the placebo condition of the 2003 study (other people); after the authors adjusted the 4-hour values to the 2003 study, their fitted curves give 13% to 25% at 4 hours, 37% to 46% at 24 hours, 56% to 73% at 48 hours and 75% to 90% at 72 hours (values between scans are read from the curves, and the adjusted 4-hour range does not match the 2003 study's 9% to 20%). In the same study, the subjective effects of injected hydromorphone were significantly smaller at 4 and 28 hours than at 52 and 76 hours, a recovery the authors call modest. The review's abstract states as results that suppressing withdrawal appears to need 50% availability or less, and that blocking the reinforcing and subjective effects of typical doses of other opioids needs less than 20% (less than 10% against higher-than-usual doses); but its body says that there is no agreed definition of a block and that the availability needed for either effect is not known, its summary says that blockade 'has not been reliably observed under BUP dosing conditions studied to date', and the 20% figure comes from preliminary modelling. The volunteers were relatively healthy, mostly men, aged 18 to 50, without depressive, psychotic or anxiety disorders or substance use disorders other than nicotine, and dependent on heroin; the authors call it unclear whether the findings apply to people seeking treatment or dependent on other opioids; fentanyl was not studied; the scans used buprenorphine without naloxone, although the authors cite data that products under the tongue with and without naloxone have similar effects; and the review reports no results on breathing or overdose, so it says nothing about the risk of overdose when other opioids are used on or after buprenorphine. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
lines.population: People dependent on heroin who were not seeking treatment, studied as inpatients in laboratory studies by the review's authors, as described in one narrative review: 3 men (Zubieta et al., 2000), 5 volunteers (Greenwald et al., 2003), 10 volunteers (Greenwald et al., 2007; 5 heavier and 5 lighter smokers) and 7 volunteers on buprenorphine with naloxone against a separate group of 8 on placebo (Comer et al., 2005); in the scan studies aged 18 to 50, many fewer women than men, relatively healthy, without depressive, psychotic or anxiety disorders or substance use disorders other than nicotine
lines.exposure: Daily sublingual buprenorphine given by the investigators (study conditions: a liquid at 2 and 16 mg a day in Zubieta et al., 2000; buprenorphine-only tablets at 32, 16 and 2 mg a day, 12 days each, in Greenwald et al., 2003; 16 mg a day for at least 14 days, then placebo, in Greenwald et al., 2007; buprenorphine with naloxone at 2/0.5, 8/2 and 32/8 mg a day, 14 days each, in Comer et al., 2005), with test doses of intranasal heroin or injected hydromorphone given by the investigators; and time since the last dose after stopping 16 mg a day
lines.comparator: Placebo in the same people (Zubieta et al., 2000; Greenwald et al., 2003; doses given in a fixed order); the placebo condition of the 2003 study, in other people (Greenwald et al., 2007); a separate group of 8 heroin-detoxified volunteers on placebo (Comer et al., 2005); earlier against later times after the last dose
lines.outcome: Brain µ-opioid receptor availability (the share free to bind the PET tracer [11C]-carfentanil, as a percentage of placebo) 4 hours after the daily dose or 4 to 76 hours after the last dose; receptor availability estimated by a model from heroin self-administration and ratings (Comer et al., 2005); self-administration and subjective effects of heroin or hydromorphone; the availability thresholds for suppressing withdrawal and for blocking other opioids that the authors infer
lines.magnitude: Greenwald et al. (2014), the authors' summaries and re-analyses of their own studies; no intervals or test statistics printed. Availability, % of placebo, 4 hours after the daily dose: Zubieta et al. (2000; n = 3; liquid) 50–64% at 2 mg/day and 5–21% at 16 mg/day across regions; Greenwald et al. (2003; n = 5; tablets; range of means across seven regions) 53–72% at 2 mg, 9–20% at 16 mg, 2–12% at 32 mg; curve-fit estimates for doses not studied 71–85% (1 mg), 36–55% (4 mg), 20–35% (8 mg; 12–33% in the Fig. 1 legend), 13–24% (12 mg), 4–15% (24 mg). Comer et al. (2005; 7 on buprenorphine/naloxone against 8 on placebo; tested 15 hours after the dose; modelled from behaviour, not imaged): 21–31% (2/0.5 mg), 11–22% (8/2 mg), 6–12% (32/8 mg). After stopping 16 mg/day (Greenwald et al., 2007; n = 10): against the 2003 placebo condition 27–31% at 4 h, 54–61% at 28 h, 65–75% at 52 h and 77–94% at 76 h; adjusted curve estimates 13–25% (4 h), 19–30% (8 h), 24–36% (12 h), 29–41% (16 h), 37–46% (24 h), 56–73% (48 h), 75–90% (72 h); subjective effects of hydromorphone 24 mg intramuscularly significantly smaller at 4 and 28 h than at 52 and 76 h (no statistics printed). Variation between people (2003 study): coefficients of variation at 16 and 32 mg/day 24% and 21% for availability, 39% and 54% for plasma levels, 129% and 109% for withdrawal symptoms; a 3.5-fold range of availability at 2 mg/day in most regions. Heavier smokers (20 or more cigarettes a day, n = 5) had significantly lower availability than lighter smokers (15 or fewer, n = 5) in the 2007 study. Thresholds in the abstract and summary, inferences rather than measurements: withdrawal suppression at 50% availability or less (trough plasma level at least 1 ng/mL); blockade of typical doses below 20% (trough at least 3 ng/mL), from preliminary modelling; below 10% against higher-than-usual doses.
lines.reasoning: As the review describes them, the primary studies are within-person comparisons with placebo given in a fixed order, a time course without a concurrent control and a comparison with a separate group, so the evidence starts low (METHODS 6.3: within-person laboratory studies start high only when the order was randomized or counterbalanced, and a claim seen only through reviews starts from the design of the primary studies). Down one level each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision: very low (the floor is reached at the first downgrade; the others are recorded for their reasons). The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft and its statement says the figures are second-hand (METHODS 6.3). Status replicated by the same team: the fall in availability with dose was seen in two scan studies (3 and 5 people) and incomplete blockade in several studies, all by overlapping authors; the time course after stopping rests on one study of 10 people. The abstract's thresholds are reported as the authors' inferences, not as findings. The doses are the studies' conditions; the claim gives no dosing advice and no timing for using other opioids.

lines.q: Does Suboxone block other opioids, and for how long?
lines.short: Only partly. In small lab studies, even high doses didn't fully block heroin or another opioid. After the last dose, scans over the next 3 days showed more opioid receptors free each day.
lines.but: Each study had 3 to 10 volunteers on heroin, not in treatment. Fentanyl and overdose weren't studied.
how: In brain scans of people dependent on heroin, buprenorphine (Suboxone's main drug) took up more opioid receptors as the daily dose went up. At 16 mg a day, 9 to 20 in 100 were still free 4 hours after a dose.
Even at the highest doses tested, heroin and another opioid still had some effect. The review mentions people who take more of them to get past the block, but has no data on what happens then.
After 10 volunteers stopped 16 mg a day, free receptors rose from about 13 to 25 in 100 at 4 hours to about 75 to 90 in 100 at 3 days. These figures come from curves drawn between 4 scans.
The review's summary gives receptor levels needed to block other opioids. But its own authors say nobody knows them. A full block was never reliably seen.

lines.statement: In people in the USA who stopped taking prescribed tramadol in its first five years on the market (April 1995 to March 2000), withdrawal was reported, mostly as ordinary opioid withdrawal and, in about 1 in 8 reported cases, with symptoms not usual in opioid withdrawal, such as severe anxiety and panic, confusion or feelings of unreality, numbness or tingling, and hallucinations; these are reported cases only, with no comparison group, so how often withdrawal follows stopping tramadol, and whether it differs from withdrawal from other opioids measured the same way, are not known. A committee that the manufacturer set up on the recommendation of an FDA advisory committee classified 1,248 adverse-event reports that reached the company or the FDA, or a paid network of 255 drug researchers, clinicians and counsellors (average response 48.7%), using ratings based on DSM-IV (Senay et al., 2003). Withdrawal was rated only where there was no drug-seeking: 422 reports (33 in 100 of all reports by Table 3; the abstract says nearly 40), of which 367 were 'typical', with at least three DSM-IV opioid withdrawal symptoms such as stomach cramps, diarrhoea, goose flesh, a runny nose, sweating, restlessness and poor sleep, and 55 'atypical' (13 in 100 of withdrawal reports, about 1 in 8): opioid-type withdrawal with a strong component of other symptoms. Among these 55, severe anxiety and panic attacks were reported in 32.8%, confusion, delusions, depersonalization, derealization or paranoia in 27.2%, numbness, tingling or ringing in the ears in 25.4%, and hallucinations of touch, sight or hearing in 20.0%. Another 124 reports, rated as 'abuse' because of drug-seeking, also described withdrawal (121 typical, 3 atypical), so at least 546 reports described it. Of typical cases with a known dose (63 in 100), 92 in 100 had taken at most 400 mg a day, which the authors give as the maximum recommended dose (range 50 to 2,000 mg), and many cases followed only 3 or 4 days of use (exposure known for about half; no counts); a quarter of atypical cases (dose known for 78 in 100) had taken more than 400 mg a day, against 8 in 100 of typical cases (no counts or test). Withdrawal followed sudden stopping, which the authors say many doctors did despite the label's warning, and in some cases a gradual reduction. Doctors described most reported cases as mild and usually over in 2 or 3 days, and the committee says atypical cases tended to last longer and to be harder to manage (no counts; it also drew on about 75 consultations). The authors say the atypical symptoms resembled those reported on stopping SSRI antidepressants more than opioid withdrawal, suggest, without testing it, a link with tramadol's effects on serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake, and warn that they could be mistaken for psychosis or delirium; apart from the higher doses, they found nothing that told who would have them. Limits: the cases are reports someone chose to make, with no count of the people who stopped without withdrawal and no group stopping another opioid; the reporting rate peaked at about 2.3 reported cases per 100,000 people estimated to have been prescribed tramadol in a quarter (read from the figure; 2.5 to 3.0 in the text) and later fell below 1, the authors also give about 1 and under 2 per 100,000, and they cite an FDA estimate that spontaneous reports capture only about 10 in 100 adverse events and say that after several years they probably capture well under 5 in 100, so these rates are minimums, not how often withdrawal happens; age was known for 139 of 455 cases (a total that matches neither 422 nor 546), sex for 82 to 87 in 100 (about 56 in 100 of them women) and the dose for 63 to 78 in 100; other medicines, antidepressants among them, and earlier drug use were not reported; the 'atypical' category was created during the study and every case was rescored, with no check of agreement between raters, and it is described both as always coming with typical symptoms and as sometimes replacing them; reports with drug-seeking were counted as 'abuse', not withdrawal; no statistical test is reported; and the work was funded by a grant from the manufacturer, and the article has no conflict-of-interest statement. A systematic review of Iranian studies (Rostam-Abadi et al., 2020) describes two case reports of tramadol withdrawal: a man who sought help with mental and physical symptoms 2 weeks after suddenly stopping tramadol he had taken for 2 years, all gone within a few days (its reference list titles the report as psychosis following tramadol withdrawal), and a newborn with vomiting, poor feeding, tremor and seizures whose mother had taken tramadol for back pain during pregnancy; it describes no study of how often withdrawal follows stopping tramadol. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People in the USA prescribed tramadol (Ultram) in its first five years on the market (April 1995 to March 2000) whose withdrawal after stopping or reducing it was reported to the manufacturer, the FDA (MedWatch) or a paid network of 255 drug researchers, clinicians and counsellors; in Iran, two case reports (an adult and a newborn)
lines.exposure: Stopping tramadol, mostly suddenly and in some reports gradually (reported daily amounts, where known, 50–2,000 mg in typical and 50–1,300 mg in atypical cases)
lines.comparator: None: no people who stopped tramadol without withdrawal and no people stopping another opioid; 'typical' and 'atypical' reports compared descriptively, 'atypical' defined against the DSM-IV list of opioid withdrawal symptoms
lines.outcome: Withdrawal as classified by the committee from reports: 'typical' opioid withdrawal (at least three DSM-IV opioid withdrawal symptoms, no drug-seeking) and 'atypical' withdrawal (opioid-type withdrawal with other nervous-system symptoms); the share of each symptom group among atypical cases; reported cases per 100,000 people estimated to be prescribed
lines.magnitude: Senay et al. (2003), adverse-event reports from April 1995 to March 2000: 1,248 classified; 422 rated withdrawal without drug-seeking (Table 3: 33%; editors' calculation 33.8%; abstract and Discussion: nearly 40%): typical 367 (86.97%), atypical 55 (13.03%; about 1 in 8; typical to atypical about 7 to 1); of 644 reports rated as 'abuse', 124 also had withdrawal symptoms (121 typical, 3 atypical), at least 546 in all (43.8% of 1,248, editors' calculation). Among the 55 atypical: severe anxiety and panic 32.8%, unusual CNS symptoms 27.2%, unusual sensory phenomena 25.4%, hallucinations 20.0% (as printed; the nearest counts of 55 give 32.7%, 27.3%, 25.5% and 20.0%, editors' calculation; the total exceeds 100%). Dose known in 63% of typical cases (50–2,000 mg a day; 92% at or below 400 mg) and 78% of atypical cases (50–1,300 mg; 25% above 400 mg, against 8% of typical; no counts); exposure known in about 50%, many of 3–4 days (no counts). Reporting rate per 100,000 people estimated to be prescribed: peak about 2.3 in the quarter centred on May 1996 (37 typical, 10 atypical reports; read from Figure 1), 2.5–3.0 in the text; later below 1 (last quarter about 0.3); approximately 1 (p. 238) and less than 2 (p. 239) in the Discussion; capture of spontaneous reports cited as about 10%, later under 5%. Sex known in 82% and 87%, about 56% women. Rostam-Abadi et al. (2020): two Iranian case reports (an adult; a newborn); no study of withdrawal frequency.
lines.reasoning: Descriptive (what reported cases contained): starts low; down two levels for risk of bias; very low. Status single study: one surveillance series; the Iranian review adds two case reports and no study of how often withdrawal follows stopping. The rates per 100,000 are reported cases over estimated prescriptions, with a capture the authors themselves put at about 10 in 100 or less, so they are given only as minimums. Whether the 'atypical' symptoms are particular to tramadol was not tested: no group stopping another opioid was studied; and the abstract's nearly 40% is 33 in 100 by Table 3. Not read: the committee's earlier report on the same programme (Cicero et al., 1999, Drug and Alcohol Dependence 57, 7–22) and Raffa et al. (1992) on tramadol's mechanisms.

lines.q: Is tramadol withdrawal different from other opioids?
lines.short: Sometimes, going by reports. In US reports from 1995 to 2000, most looked like usual opioid withdrawal. But about 1 in 8 also had panic, confusion, numbness or hallucinations.
lines.but: It's only cases people chose to report. And no one compared it with stopping other opioids.
how: Of 1,248 side-effect reports in tramadol's first five years in the US, 422 were withdrawal after stopping. Most were the usual kind: cramps, diarrhoea, goose bumps, a runny nose, sweating, poor sleep.

55 (about 1 in 8) had more: bad anxiety or panic (1 in 3 of them), confusion or feeling unreal (1 in 4), numbness or tingling (1 in 4), or hallucinations (1 in 5). The researchers say this could be mistaken for psychosis.
Most people whose dose was known had taken no more than the recommended daily maximum, and many had used tramadol only a few days. Doctors called most cases mild, usually over in 2 or 3 days.

How often withdrawal happens is unknown: the researchers cite an estimate that only about 1 in 10 side effects get reported. The drug's maker paid for the study. A review of Iranian studies found just two case reports of it.
